metadata.copyright_and_use_note: This file is an original explanatory, comparative, and implementation-oriented teaching aid. It paraphrases publicly documented structures and does not reproduce complete commercial move lists, playbooks, setting text, or proprietary examples.

pbta_label_policy.summary: The PbtA label is self-applied by a creator whose game is meaningfully inspired by Apocalypse World and who follows the creators' publishing policy.
pbta_label_policy.inspiration: A creator may publish a game inspired by Apocalypse World without needing permission merely for the inspiration.
pbta_label_policy.exact_words: Using protected wording can require permission or a license.
pbta_label_policy.logo: The official policy asks creators to request permission before using the PbtA logo.
pbta_label_policy.recommended_credit: Credit Apocalypse World and its creators in thanks, notes, or credits when it is a meaningful inspiration.

redistribution_checklist: Separate ideas and original paraphrase from copied wording.
Read each source's current license rather than assuming all PbtA games share one.
Request permission for logos, art, trade dress, or protected text when required.
Do not describe this database as official or publisher-endorsed.
licensing.source_specific_warning: Open licenses vary by game and edition. A license attached to one PbtA game does not license another game's text.

edition_and_family_identity.direct_answer: Powered by the Apocalypse is not a single game system with one universal edition. It is a self-applied family label for games inspired by Apocalypse World or by other PbtA games.

five_minute_explanation.one_sentence: Describe what the characters do in the fiction; when a rule or move applies, follow it exactly; let the result change the situation; then continue the conversation and play to find out what happens.
core_loop: The GM or another player describes the current fictional situation.
A player says what their character does, wants, asks, or attempts.
The table determines whether a move or other rule applies.
If no rule applies, resolve the action through the established fiction and continue.
If a move applies, follow its procedure, including any roll, choices, questions, costs, or automatic effects.
Apply the result as a real change in the fiction.
The GM and players describe the consequences, shift the spotlight, and ask what happens next.
five_minute_explanation.most_important_difference_from_many_trad: Players normally do not select a generic skill check whenever they attempt something uncertain. Rolls happen when the fiction and the game's rules bring a move into play.
five_minute_explanation.best_beginner_rule: Do not begin with the dice. Begin by saying what the character actually does.

before_play.instruction: Choose one specific PbtA game whose premise matches the story the group wants.
before_play.why: PbtA games are tightly designed around particular genres, conflicts, and themes.

before_play.instruction: Read that game's premise, player principles, basic moves, playbooks, and GM agenda/principles.
before_play.why: The exact text determines what the game is about and how authority is shared.

before_play.instruction: Hold a session-zero conversation about tone, subject matter, safety tools, campaign length, and the kinds of conflict everyone wants.
before_play.why: Many PbtA games create emotionally charged, interpersonal, horrific, romantic, political, or violent situations.

before_play.instruction: Choose playbooks or other character frameworks, then follow the game's creation steps in order.
before_play.why: Character creation often creates the setting, relationships, and opening situation at the same time.

before_play.instruction: Answer relationship and setting questions aloud, recording only what the game asks you to record.
before_play.why: The group's answers are usable fiction, not decorative backstory.

during_play.instruction: The facilitator frames an immediate situation and asks a character what they do.
The player answers in fictional terms, not only with a move name.
When a move applies, resolve it and make every listed choice or consequence matter.
On a mixed result or miss, change the situation instead of stalling or merely saying 'nothing happens.'
End scenes and sessions using the game's own recovery, experience, relationship, and end-of-session procedures.

minimum_materials: The chosen game's rulebook or quickstart
Its current basic-move and GM reference sheets
One character playbook or sheet per player, when the game uses them
The dice, cards, tokens, or other randomizer specified by that game
A way to record conditions, harm, resources, relationships, clocks, or experience

expectation_reset: You may roll less often, but each roll can have broader consequences.
A 7-9 is usually a hit with a cost, complication, reduced effect, or hard choice, not simply a failed roll.
A miss gives the game permission to change the situation; it does not always mean the character looked incompetent.
The GM may not roll dice at all.
Combat may use the same conversation and move structure as every other scene.
Your playbook is a dramatic role and pressure structure, not only a combat class.
minimum_first_read: the selected playbook or character framework

priority_order.rule: Pause, revise, skip, or stop regardless of fictional or mechanical continuity.
Use the exact edition, playtest packet, playbook, move sheet, and official corrections selected by the table.
A move, playbook feature, or subsystem that directly addresses the situation normally overrides general guidance.
Honor facts already established and the game's division of who may answer each question.
When text remains ambiguous, make a visible temporary ruling consistent with agenda and principles.
Use this file for shared habits, comparison, teaching, and implementation only; it never overrides the chosen game.

conflict_resolution_procedure: Stop before applying an irreversible consequence if the disagreement is material.
Identify the exact rule, move, playbook, edition, and version.
State the established fictional facts and player intent.
Identify who the rules authorize to decide or answer.
Apply specific text before general expectations imported from another game.
If ambiguity remains, choose the ruling that best preserves earned outcomes, transparency, and the game's agenda.
Record the ruling if it is likely to recur and review it after the session.

states.entry: A scene begins or the previous result creates a new situation.
actions: describe immediate sensory and social facts
states.exit: A player is invited to act or answer.

actions: describe what the character actually does
states.exit: The table can judge possibility and triggers.

actions: check access, tools, scale, leverage, timing, and opposition
identify automatic, impossible, or rule-triggering outcomes
states.exit: Choose automatic resolution, repositioning, or a specific procedure.

actions: roll, draw, compare, spend, choose, or ask as instructed
states.exit: The rule's mechanical output is complete.

states.entry: The players look to the world, a miss grants response, or prepared pressure acts.
states.exit: A new opportunity, danger, or question is visible.

states.entry: The current beat has changed the situation.
actions: stay with the character if an immediate choice remains
return to an unresolved concurrent scene
close or transition when the scene's question is answered

terminal_or_transition_states.condition: The scene's central question is answered or pressure moves elsewhere.
terminal_or_transition_states.next: frame another scene, montage, downtime, or session procedure.

terminal_or_transition_states.condition: The planned time or a strong dramatic turn is reached.
terminal_or_transition_states.next: apply end-of-session, recovery, relationship, growth, and campaign-state rules.

terminal_or_transition_states.condition: The premise resolves, the group chooses to stop, or the game's end condition occurs.
terminal_or_transition_states.next: resolve epilogues, retirement, legacy, and unresolved safety or debrief needs.

invariants: Do not randomize before the relevant fictional action or procedure exists.
Do not leave a move result only as a number.
Do not revoke a promised success because it disrupts preparation.
Do not let a facilitator consequence contradict a protection already granted.
Do not continue past a real-world safety stop.

is: A family of games connected by inspiration and self-identification.
An approach in which procedures shape a focused conversation about a particular kind of fiction.
A tradition of designing rules, moves, playbooks, GM instructions, and advancement around the game's themes.
A style that often distributes narrative authority through explicit questions, options, and procedures.
A family in which consequences normally create forward motion.
is_not: A universal open rules engine with one canonical rulebook.
Required to use playbooks, moves, stats, or a traditional GM.
A guarantee that two PbtA games are mechanically compatible.
An instruction to improvise without rules or preparation.
A license to ignore the exact wording of the chosen game's procedures.
what_pbta_is_and_is_not.self_identification_rule: A game's creator is the relevant authority on whether the game is PbtA, because the label describes its inspiration.

core_play_principles.name: The conversation is the base system
core_play_principles.explanation: Play is an exchange of descriptions, questions, decisions, reactions, and procedures. Character sheets and dice enter the conversation when called upon, then hand play back to the fiction.

core_play_principles.name: Fiction and mechanics continually affect each other
core_play_principles.explanation: Fictional facts determine whether an action is possible, dangerous, costly, or move-triggering. Mechanical results create new fictional facts that must be honored.

core_play_principles.name: Play to find out
core_play_principles.explanation: Prepare pressures, people, threats, places, and motives, but do not decide the protagonists' choices or the final outcome in advance.

core_play_principles.name: Use specific procedures instead of defaulting to generic checks
core_play_principles.explanation: A roll is justified by the chosen game's move or procedure, not merely by uncertainty.

core_play_principles.name: Every result changes the situation
core_play_principles.explanation: A strong hit, mixed result, miss, automatic effect, spent resource, or chosen option should become visible in what happens next.

core_play_principles.name: Honor the move's exact promises
core_play_principles.explanation: When a move grants questions, choices, protection, harm, information, or authority, provide it. Do not secretly weaken a success because the GM preferred another outcome.

core_play_principles.name: Fictional positioning matters before and after the roll
core_play_principles.explanation: The character's approach, tools, leverage, location, relationships, and opposition can determine whether a move can happen and what its result can accomplish.

core_play_principles.name: Share the spotlight
core_play_principles.explanation: Move between characters at moments of tension, invite quieter players, and avoid letting one player make every decision or roll.

core_play_principles.name: Questions and answers are often mechanical procedures
core_play_principles.explanation: When the rules require an honest answer or a specific question, that exchange is part of resolution, not optional flavor.

core_play_principles.name: Genre is built into the rules
core_play_principles.explanation: A PbtA game's moves identify the actions, dilemmas, relationships, and consequences that the game wants to revisit.

core_play_principles.name: Rules are a shared agreement with humane flexibility
core_play_principles.explanation: Current Apocalypse World 3rd Edition preview commentary describes moves as frameworks with designed tolerance. The group may discuss a move when its strict application does not land, but should preserve the game's underlying purpose and return to the written rule as the stable baseline.

responsibilities: Portray a protagonist honestly and actively.
Say what the character does in the fiction.
Follow mandatory move triggers and procedures.
Make choices granted by moves.
Answer questions truthfully when the rules require it.
Track the resources assigned to the player.
Respect the established fiction and other players' authority over their own characters.
Pursue the playbook's pressures, relationships, drives, or themes rather than trying to avoid every complication.
not_responsible_for: Protecting the character from all trouble.
Winning through optimal action-economy play unless the specific game explicitly centers that.

responsibilities: Follow the chosen game's agenda, principles, rules, and GM moves.
Describe the world and portray non-player characters.
Ask questions and use the answers.
Present pressures and consequences without predetermining the protagonists' choices.
Apply the results of player moves honestly.
Make GM moves when the game instructs or the conversation demands a response.
Keep events moving and distribute spotlight.
Prepare only the kinds of material the game requests.
not_responsible_for: Writing a fixed plot that the players must follow.
Rolling to oppose every player action unless the game explicitly says so.
Hiding all relevant stakes until after a choice.
Neutral refereeing divorced from the game's agenda and principles.

gm_less_and_coop_variants.note: Some PbtA games are GMless, co-GMed, solo, or use rotating authority.
procedure: Identify who answers each category of question.
Use oracles, prompts, cards, structured scenes, or shared roles exactly as the game directs.
Do not import a traditional GM by default when the game intentionally distributes that authority.

goals: Confirm the exact game and edition or playtest version.
Explain the premise in one or two sentences.
Agree on campaign or one-shot length.
Discuss tone, intensity, humor, romance, horror, violence, and intra-party conflict.
Choose safety tools and establish how anyone can pause, revise, or remove content.
Explain whether player-versus-player moves are possible and how consent will be handled.
Explain what information players control about their own characters.
Review the basic moves and the GM agenda.
Create characters together so relationship questions can be answered in context.
Record unresolved questions as material to discover during play, not as errors to eliminate.

recommended_categories: veils: content that may exist but is not described in detail
aftercare and debrief for intense sessions
check-ins when a move would control, alter, expose, or pressure another player character
safety_baseline.important_note: Safety procedures supplement the game's rules and can always interrupt them.

expectation_reset_for_traditional_rpg_pl: You may roll less often, but each roll can have broader consequences.
A 7-9 is usually a hit with a cost, complication, reduced effect, or hard choice, not simply a failed roll.
A miss gives the game permission to change the situation; it does not always mean the character looked incompetent.
The GM may not roll dice at all.
Combat may use the same conversation and move structure as every other scene.
Your playbook is a dramatic role and pressure structure, not only a combat class.

character_creation.universal_warning: There is no universal PbtA character-creation method. Use the ordered steps on the chosen game's playbook or sheet.

common_components.purpose: Focuses the character's dramatic role, resources, special moves, and likely conflicts.
Creates an immediately playable person rather than a stat block.
Modify moves or represent changing self-concepts, competencies, emotions, or methods.
Give the character distinctive permissions, procedures, and ways to affect the conversation.
Mechanically connect protagonists and create immediate reasons to interact.
Establish fictional permissions, tags, scarcity, and signature capabilities.
Create setting details, vulnerabilities, goals, and material the GM should bring into play.
Define how danger, pressure, sacrifice, or limited protection works in that game.

best_practices: Create characters in the same room or call whenever possible.
Read the playbook introduction and all chosen moves.
Do not assume two playbooks with similar powers tell the same kind of story.
Treat every relationship answer as permission to create scenes around it.
Leave blanks that the rules intend the group to discover later.
Avoid writing a private novel-length backstory that conflicts with group creation.

choose_by: the kind of pressure you want the character to face
the relationships you want to explore
the decisions you want to make repeatedly
the genre role you want to embody
do_not_choose_only_by: a superficial resemblance to a class in another RPG

questions: Where is everyone?
What is happening right now?
What is immediately obvious?
What has already been established as true?

cycle.procedure: The GM or current speaker asks what a character does, or a player takes initiative by describing an action.

questions: What are you trying to accomplish?
How are you doing it?
What tools, leverage, or position are you relying on?
What danger or resistance is present?

cycle.procedure: Determine whether a move, resource rule, harm rule, relationship rule, or other procedure applies.
Follow the procedure completely, including choices and questions.
Describe how the mechanical result appears in the fiction.
Shift the situation, spotlight, or stakes and ask what happens next.

possible_outcomes: The action simply happens because the fiction permits it.
The GM explains why it cannot happen under the established circumstances.
The GM states the possible consequence or required fictional step and asks what the player does.
Another character or threat reacts according to the fiction.
The table asks for more detail until it is clear whether a move applies.
when_no_move_triggers.do_not: Invent a generic 2d6 roll merely because the outcome feels uncertain, unless the chosen game gives a catch-all move or explicit rule for doing so.

moves.definition: A move is a rule that organizes part of the conversation. It may be triggered by fiction, chosen directly, invoked by procedure, or operate without a fictional trigger.

common_anatomy.trigger_or_timing: When, whether, or how the move enters play.
common_anatomy.fictional_requirements: What must be true, what the character must actually do, and what target or situation must exist.
common_anatomy.mechanical_instruction: Roll, choose, spend, ask, hold, mark, compare, draw, or apply an automatic effect.
common_anatomy.result_branches: What happens on each result band or choice.
common_anatomy.authority: Who chooses, answers, or describes each part.
common_anatomy.follow_through: How the result changes ongoing fiction.

trigger_patterns.description: The move becomes mandatory when its described event happens in the fiction.
trigger_patterns.table_habit: Anyone may point out that the trigger has occurred; pause and resolve it.

trigger_patterns.description: The player can intentionally have the character take the action named by the move.
trigger_patterns.table_habit: Clarify what the character does, confirm fictional permission, then use the move.

trigger_patterns.description: The move occurs at session start, session end, when harm is suffered, when a resource changes, or at another rules-defined time.
The player may invoke the move without first satisfying a fictional trigger, when the move says so.
An instruction for how the GM changes or responds to the fiction; normally narrated as events rather than announced by rule name.

traditional_to_do_it_do_it_guidance.meaning: When a move has a fictional trigger, the character must actually do the triggering thing in the fiction; conversely, when the character does it, the group should not skip the move.
does_not_mean: The player must quote the move's title.
The player can press a move like a video-game button without describing an approach.
The GM may deny a clearly triggered move merely to preserve a planned outcome.

disagreement_procedure.current_apocalypse_world_3e_preview_infl: Official 2026 preview commentary instructs participants who disagree about a move to explain themselves and pause until they work it out.
system_neutral_steps: Pause the fiction before adding new consequences.
Each person explains what they believe the move requires or promises.
Check the move text, surrounding rules, agenda, and principles.
Clarify the fictional facts and each person's intended outcome.
Agree on the written interpretation, a mutually acceptable exception, or a return to the strict written baseline.
Use a safety tool or stop the scene if the disagreement concerns boundaries or player agency.

result_integrity: Do not make a player roll again to receive the success already granted.
Do not convert every strong hit into a hidden complication.
Do not treat every miss as the literal opposite of the attempted action.
Do not omit choices or questions because the GM thinks the answer is obvious.
Do not let an option exceed what the established fiction can coherently support without discussing it.

classic_2d6_resolution.status: Common and historically important, but not universal to PbtA.
classic_2d6_resolution.formula: Roll 2d6 and add the stat or modifier named by the move.

typical_result_bands.label: strong hit
typical_result_bands.generic_meaning: The move's strongest listed result applies, often with greater effect, more choices, or fewer costs.

typical_result_bands.label: weak hit or mixed result
typical_result_bands.generic_meaning: The move succeeds according to its text, but with reduced effect, a cost, exposure, a complication, a choice, or shared authority.

typical_result_bands.label: miss
typical_result_bands.generic_meaning: Follow the move's miss text. When it has no explicit miss clause, the GM commonly makes an appropriate move according to the game's rules.

typical_result_bands.label: advanced or exceptional result in some games
typical_result_bands.generic_meaning: Only applies when the chosen game or an advanced move explicitly defines it.

critical_rolls.natural_12: Usually has no special meaning by itself unless the game says it does.
critical_rolls.snake_eyes: Usually has no special meaning by itself unless the game says it does.
critical_rolls.rule: Read the final modified total and the move's text.

probability_table.assumptions: Unmodified 2d6 distribution; no rerolls, advantage systems, bonuses after the roll, or move-specific alterations.
interpretation: At +0, a strong hit occurs 16.67% of the time, a 7-9 occurs 41.67%, and a miss occurs 41.67%.
At +1, the most common band is 7-9 at 44.44%.
At +3, strong hits become more likely than the other bands, but misses still occur 8.33% of the time.
Small modifiers are powerful because they shift results across two thresholds.

advanced_12_plus_probability.warning: A 12+ result is not universal and often requires an advanced move.

rolling_procedure: Confirm the move and its named modifier.
Clarify any relevant fictional facts before rolling.
Apply only bonuses and penalties authorized by the game.
Make every required choice and answer every required question.
Describe and apply the result before making another roll.

mixed_results.not_a_generic_rule: There is no universal menu of partial-success complications.
mixed_results.correct_method: Use the exact 7-9 text of the move.
common_forms: the GM chooses part of the result
the player chooses an unwanted consequence

not_always_failure: The character may accomplish the immediate task but expose themselves to a worse problem.
The GM may reveal unwelcome information.
A resource may be lost or depleted.
The action may separate characters or put someone in a spot.
The move's own miss clause may grant a limited effect.
Another authority may describe what goes wrong.
misses.best_test: Choose a consequence that follows from the established fiction, honors the game's agenda and principles, and creates a meaningful next decision.

non_2d6_variants.core_fact: PbtA games may use other dice, dice pools, cards, tokens, diceless procedures, scene structures, or no randomizer.

documented_examples.variation: Uses an Apocalypse World-like three-band roll but assigns modifiers to individual 'plays' rather than character stats.
Uses cards and cumulative card values rather than the classic 2d6 roll.

non_2d6_variants.adaptation_rule: Do not translate a non-2d6 PbtA game back into 2d6 unless deliberately designing a hack. Follow its native procedure.

fictional_positioning.definition: The established circumstances that determine what actions are possible, what rules apply, and what an outcome can reasonably accomplish.

dimensions.question: Can the character do this at all with their current abilities, access, and tools?
Does this approach satisfy the move's conditions?
What can this action meaningfully change?
What can the opposition or environment do in response?
Is the character acting against one person, a gang, an institution, a storm, or an army?
What reason, evidence, relationship, threat, promise, or vulnerability makes the action effective?
What do range, area, messy, armor, magical, intimate, loud, or other game-specific tags establish?

examples.situation: A locked office door with ordinary tools and no immediate pressure.
examples.likely_handling: The character may simply open it after enough time, or the GM may ask how they obtain the needed tools; no move is automatically required.

examples.situation: The same lock while guards approach and alarms are active.
examples.likely_handling: A danger- or pressure-related move may trigger because the risk is now part of the action.

examples.situation: A character shoots an unaware, helpless target at point-blank range.
examples.likely_handling: Some games apply harm as established rather than using a symmetric combat roll.

examples.situation: A character tries to command a ruler with no status, leverage, threat, or supernatural power.
examples.likely_handling: A manipulation move may not trigger; the fiction may require leverage first.

forward.typical_meaning: A bonus or penalty to the next qualifying roll, then it is consumed.
forward.warning: Exact duration and qualification are game-specific.

ongoing.typical_meaning: A bonus or penalty that applies repeatedly while a stated condition remains true.
ongoing.warning: Do not assume it applies to every roll.

hold.typical_meaning: A temporary currency generated by a move and spent on that move's listed effects.
hold.rule: Unspent hold lasts only as long as the move says.

take_plus_one.typical_meaning: Add one to the specified roll or category of rolls.

mark.typical_meaning: Record a box, condition, experience, harm, resource, or other change.

as_established.typical_meaning: Use the harm, position, scale, tags, and consequences already made true in the fiction and rules.

choice_menu.typical_meaning: Select exactly the number of options granted; unchosen options are not automatically true.

ask_questions.typical_meaning: Spend the granted questions or hold and receive the honest information promised by the move.

conditions.typical_meaning: Named emotional, physical, social, or narrative states that affect play and have specific clearing procedures.

tags.typical_meaning: Compact descriptors that create fictional and sometimes numerical effects.

clock_or_countdown.typical_meaning: A structured display of worsening threat, progress, scarcity, or approaching events.

strings_bonds_hx_influence_debts.typical_meaning: Different games' relationship currencies or ratings.

combat_and_danger.universal_warning: There is no universal PbtA combat system.
common_characteristics: Combat usually remains part of the same conversation used for every other scene.
Many games have no separate initiative roll or fixed turn order.
The GM may not roll attacks for NPCs.
One move can represent a moment, exchange, chase segment, tactical objective, or whole skirmish depending on the game and fiction.
Harm may be exchanged automatically when a move says so.
Position, range, cover, weapons, armor, numbers, and intent matter through fiction and tags.
Enemies may be represented by moves, harm capacity, conditions, clocks, qualities, or narrative permissions rather than full player-style stat blocks.
combat_procedure: Establish positions, goals, immediate threats, and what is at stake.
Ask a player what their character does.
Identify the move or rule, if any, that matches the action and situation.
Resolve it once; do not divide one coherent action into unnecessary sub-rolls.
Apply harm, conditions, costs, separation, lost position, or other effects as written.
Describe the enemy and environment's response through GM moves or the result text.
Shift spotlight before one character monopolizes the whole fight.
End the fight when the fiction says the objective is achieved, abandoned, or impossible.

initiative.default_assumption: No universal initiative or action economy.
spotlight_method: Give threatened characters a chance to respond when appropriate.
Return to players who have not acted recently.
Use the game's specific battle procedures when they override free spotlight management.

enemy_actions.common_method: The GM describes an incoming threat, consequence, or completed action according to the game's GM-move rules.

distinguish.soft_move: Signals danger, offers an opportunity, or presents a consequence that the players can still address.
distinguish.hard_move: Makes an immediate, concrete, difficult-to-reverse consequence happen.

enemy_actions.warning: Soft and hard are descriptive concepts, not universal formal labels in every game.

avoid: Calling for repeated attack rolls until hit points reach zero unless the game is designed that way.
Giving NPCs a hidden traditional action economy.
Ignoring a strong hit because an enemy was intended to survive.
Assuming combat is the only place where moves can have severe consequences.
Using harm as the only meaningful stake.

harm_conditions_and_recovery.universal_warning: Every chosen game defines its own danger and recovery model.
possible_models: retirement, transformation, or loss of control
how_to_apply: Use the amount or condition established by the move, weapon, threat, or fiction.
Apply armor or reduction only where the game allows.
Describe the concrete effect, not only the marked box.
Use any required harm move, condition move, or instability procedure.
Follow the exact recovery trigger and do not import rests from another RPG.

monster_of_the_week_example_as_variation.purpose: Demonstrates how one current PbtA game combines a harm track, armor, instability, Luck, and experience.
summary: Armor reduces harm by its rating.
Serious wounds can become unstable and worsen without treatment.
Luck can alter a roll or negate a wound, but is limited.
Experience can be marked on misses and through end-of-session questions.

death_and_character_loss.rule: Read the chosen game's procedure before the first dangerous scene.
session_zero_questions: Does a player choose death, retirement, or transformation?
What happens to the player after a character leaves play?

relationships_and_player_vs_player.importance: Many PbtA games place relationships at the center of resolution and advancement.
pvp_guidance: Use the exact player-versus-player procedure, because many moves distinguish PCs from NPCs.
Do not let a social move erase another player's authority over their character unless the rule explicitly and consensually permits that effect.
State desired outcomes before rolling when the move asks for them.
Use safety tools for coercion, intimacy, betrayal, mind control, or identity-changing effects.
When a move grants another player a choice, preserve that choice.

advancement.universal_warning: There is no universal level system.
common_xp_triggers: fulfilling drives, keys, beliefs, playbook prompts, or relationship triggers
common_improvements: increase a stat within a cap
gain a move from another playbook
gain gear, resources, followers, territory, or a team feature
create or play an additional character
transform the campaign or character's role
best_practices: Review every XP trigger before play.
Mark experience immediately when the trigger occurs.
Choose improvements that create new fictional possibilities, not only larger numbers.
Discuss major playbook changes or retirement with the group.

core_structure.agenda: The broad outcomes and priorities the GM must pursue.
core_structure.principles: The decision-making rules that shape every description, judgment, and move.
core_structure.always_say_or_rules: Constraints on what the GM may state and what sources of truth must be honored.
core_structure.gm_moves: Concrete ways to change the fiction when the GM has the opportunity or obligation.
core_structure.prep_procedure: The game's approved method for creating threats, fronts, mysteries, arcs, factions, clocks, or situations.

classic_apocalypse_world_style_agenda_su: Make the fictional world feel real.
Make the protagonists' lives active and consequential rather than dull.
Play to find out what happens.
common_principle_patterns: Ask provocative questions and build on the answers.
Be a fan of the protagonists while making their lives difficult.
Give non-player characters names, motives, humanity, and concrete behavior.
Think about events outside the current scene.
Use consequences that follow from the fiction.
Do not speak the name of a GM move as though announcing an ability.

common_apocalypse_world_style_opportunit: A player rolls a miss and the move does not fully specify the result.
Everyone looks to the GM to learn what happens.
The players hand the GM a clear fictional opportunity.
A rule, countdown, threat, or move explicitly instructs the GM to act.
when_to_make_a_gm_move.warning: Use the chosen game's list and timing rules; some games structure facilitator actions differently.

generic_gm_move_families: reveal danger or future trouble
show off-screen consequences
separate characters
put someone in a difficult position
inflict established harm or another established cost
take away or threaten a resource
offer an opportunity with or without a cost
turn a move's consequences back toward the characters
advance a threat or countdown
present a difficult choice
tell the possible consequences and ask whether the character proceeds
shift attention to another character or location
gm_move_selection_test: Does it follow from what has already been established?
Does it respect the result the player earned?
Does it create a concrete next decision?
Is its severity appropriate to the setup and timing?
Will the players understand what changed?

soft.function: Telegraph, threaten, reveal, position, or offer a chance to respond.
examples: The bridge cables begin snapping one by one.
The detective reaches for the evidence bag.
You hear the monster in the room behind you.

hard.function: Apply an immediate and concrete consequence.
examples: The bridge gives way beneath you.
The detective takes the evidence and orders your arrest.
The monster crashes through the wall and separates you from the others.

soft_and_hard_moves.severity_rule: A hard move should normally be supported by prior setup, a miss, an ignored danger, a golden opportunity, or a rule that authorizes it.

prepare: threats and what they will do if unopposed
questions you genuinely want play to answer
countdowns, fronts, mysteries, factions, or arcs required by the game
do_not_prepare: a sequence of scenes that must occur in order
a final outcome that invalidates move results
prep.clue_guidance: Do not make essential forward progress depend on repeatedly guessing the correct question or succeeding on one hidden check. Use the game's investigation moves and threat structure to deliver actionable information and new decisions.

player_best_practices.example: Instead of saying only 'I use the manipulation move,' explain what you want and what leverage, promise, pressure, or appeal you use.
Choose actions that expose the character's conflicts and relationships rather than avoiding every trigger.
Ask what the character can see, what is dangerous, what a move requires, and what the stakes are before rolling.
A cost changes what you face; it does not require surrendering control over your character beyond what the rule grants.
Spend hold, Luck, Strings, Team, or similar resources when their fictional moment matters.
Answer the GM's questions with concrete, usable details and leave room for other players.
After a major choice or reveal, invite another character's reaction.

gm_preparation: Know the premise, agenda, principles, basic moves, and each selected playbook.
Prepare names, impressions, possible threats, and open questions rather than a plot.
Know the opening situation or follow the game's procedure for creating it.
recommended_flow: Introduce the premise and safety tools.
Summarize the relationships and immediate setting aloud.
Begin in a situation that demands a choice now.
Ask direct questions and build on answers.
Use early moves to teach the resolution bands.
Give every character a meaningful interaction.
End with the game's session-end procedure.
first_session_gm_priorities: Learn what each character cares about.
Create links between characters and threats.
Find where the group lacks control.
Avoid explaining the entire campaign before play reveals it.

setup: Use a game or quickstart designed for one-shots when available.
Preselect or limit playbooks without removing meaningful choice.
Begin after the characters are already connected.
Use one urgent situation with a visible countdown or consequence.
Use faster advancement only if the game recommends it.
pacing: First quarter: establish characters, relationships, and immediate problem.
Second quarter: reveal the deeper pressure and force tradeoffs.
Third quarter: escalate consequences and expose character conflicts.
Final quarter: resolve the central question and perform end-of-session reflection.
avoid: A long tavern-style introduction with no pressure.
Multiple unrelated threats.
Saving every important revelation for the final minutes.
Treating misses as delays.

campaign_engine: Record the consequences of player choices.
Update threats, relationships, clocks, fronts, or mysteries between sessions.
Bring unresolved costs and promises back into play.
Let advancement change the kinds of stories the characters can create.
Ask whether the original premise is still the game everyone wants.
continuity: What promise, debt, injury, condition, or resource remains unresolved?
What are we now playing to find out?
endings: Use retirement, final advancements, endgame moves, or arc procedures when provided.
Let campaigns end when their central question has been answered.
Do not force indefinite play merely because characters can still improve.

five_minute_player_explanation: Say what your character does in the story.
You roll only when a move or rule applies.
In classic 2d6 games, 10+ is a strong result, 7-9 is a hit with limits or consequences, and 6- lets the game respond strongly.
Read the move every time until it becomes familiar.
Your choices and relationships matter more than optimizing a turn sequence.
five_minute_gm_explanation: Ask questions, use the answers, and present concrete situations.
On a GM move, change the fiction and create another decision.
Honor every success and every choice granted by the rules.
teaching_during_play: Before the first roll, identify the trigger aloud.
After the roll, read the relevant result aloud.
Ask the player to choose before describing the final outcome.
Translate the result into concrete fiction.
Explain one rule at the moment it becomes relevant rather than front-loading every subsystem.

differences_between_pbta_games.compatibility_rule: A move, playbook, or subsystem from one PbtA game is not automatically balanced, meaningful, or mechanically compatible with another.

player_before_a_move: Is the target or situation present?
Do I have the fictional permission, tools, position, or leverage?
Which exact move or rule applies?
player_after_a_move: Describe your character's part of the result.
gm_before_a_response: Has a move granted or restricted my authority?
What do my agenda and principles require?
Is this a soft setup or an authorized hard consequence?
What concrete choice will this create?
gm_between_sessions: Update threats, clocks, mysteries, fronts, or factions.
Record changes caused by the protagonists.
Review character flags, conditions, relationships, and advancement.
Do not write the protagonists' solution.
session_end: Ask what threads players want to continue.
Check in about tone, boundaries, and the session experience.

validation_rules_for_a_pbta_rules_app: Require a specific game rules profile.
Do not assume 2d6 unless the profile declares it.
Store move trigger, roll, result branches, choices, authority, and follow-through separately.
Store modifiers with duration and qualification.
Treat relationship mechanics as game-specific typed resources.
Allow facilitatorless profiles.
Allow moves with no roll and rolls with no fictional trigger.
Allow result bands other than 6-/7-9/10+.
Record source edition and errata date for every imported rule.
Never merge move text from different games solely by matching names.

classic_2d6_probability_reference.warning: This mathematics describes the common 2d6 bands only. It is not a definition of PbtA and should not be used for games with another randomizer.
interpretation: Each +1 meaningfully shifts probability because 2d6 is a bell-shaped distribution.
At +0, a miss occurs on 15 of 36 outcomes, a 7–9 on 15, and a 10+ on 6.
At +3, a 10+ becomes more likely than either other band, while misses remain possible.
Very large modifiers compress or eliminate result bands and can undermine a move designed around all three outcomes.

roll_3d6_keep_highest_2.effect: Substantially favors higher results compared with ordinary 2d6.

roll_3d6_keep_lowest_2.effect: Substantially favors lower results compared with ordinary 2d6.

optional_variant_math_not_universal.design_warning: Do not add these variants merely by analogy to advantage or disadvantage; test how they interact with experience, miss moves, and 12+ results.

harm_models.name: Numeric Harm Clock
harm_models.description: Incoming harm marks a small ordered track. Higher filled segments can trigger instability, incapacitation, or death.
questions: Is harm reduced before or after it is marked?
Do NPCs use the same scale?
What happens at each threshold?
Can armor or a move change the category of harm?
harm_models.best_for: Games where violence is dangerous and consequences should accumulate visibly.
harm_models.risks: Treating the track like universal hit points can erase fictional injury details.

harm_models.name: Hit Points or Durability Pool
harm_models.description: Damage subtracts from a larger number until a threshold changes the character's state.
questions: What does the pool represent?
Are there wound penalties?
How is maximum value set?
What happens at zero?
harm_models.best_for: Games that want tactical attrition or familiar fantasy-adventure durability.
harm_models.risks: Players may focus on numerical depletion instead of fictional positioning unless the rules reconnect them.

harm_models.name: Named Conditions
harm_models.description: Characters mark specific emotional, physical, social, or supernatural states that modify moves and clear through defined actions.
questions: Are conditions chosen by the player or imposed by a result?
Can multiple conditions coexist?
What clears each one?
What happens when all are marked?
harm_models.best_for: Games about identity, emotion, relationships, or genre-specific states.
harm_models.risks: A condition becomes empty bookkeeping if it never affects portrayal or choices.

harm_models.name: Severity Levels
harm_models.description: Consequences are categorized as minor, moderate, severe, critical, or another ordered scale.
questions: Who judges severity?
Can players resist or reduce it?
Does severity determine recovery time?
Can consequences be narrative rather than physical?
harm_models.best_for: Games with flexible consequence types and explicit effect negotiation.
harm_models.risks: Inconsistent severity without clear examples can feel arbitrary.

harm_models.name: Stress and Trauma
harm_models.description: A short-term pressure pool absorbs extraordinary effort or resistance; filling it produces lasting change.
questions: What can stress purchase?
When does it clear?
How is trauma chosen?
Does trauma retire or transform a character?
harm_models.best_for: Games about desperate competence and accumulating long-term costs.
harm_models.risks: Stress can become a generic mana pool if spending it lacks fictional meaning.

harm_models.name: Harm Move or Injury Procedure
harm_models.description: Suffering harm triggers a separate roll, choice, or procedure that determines immediate consequences.
questions: Who rolls?
What modifies the roll?
Does more harm make high or low results worse?
Can the procedure create unconsciousness, loss of gear, or panic?
harm_models.best_for: Games where the unpredictability of injury matters more than precise attrition.
harm_models.risks: Players may forget the second-stage procedure unless the sheet makes it prominent.

harm_models.name: Freeform Injury Tags
harm_models.description: The table records specific injuries or impairments whose effects follow from fiction or defined tag rules.
questions: Who names the tag?
How specific should it be?
When does it block action or trigger a move?
How is it treated or removed?
harm_models.best_for: Games prioritizing concrete fiction over numeric tracks.
harm_models.risks: Uneven interpretation can make similar injuries have very different weight.

harm_models.name: Multiple Thematic Harm Tracks
harm_models.description: Different tracks represent distinct pressures such as injury, exhaustion, depletion, reputation, or spirit.
questions: Which consequences map to which track?
Can one track spill into another?
What happens when each fills?
Which moves recover each track?
harm_models.best_for: Games where several kinds of vulnerability deserve equal mechanical weight.
harm_models.risks: Too many tracks can overload players unless each is used often and clearly.

harm_models.name: Condition-Specific Moves
harm_models.description: A marked state changes available moves or triggers a special procedure when acted upon.
questions: Does the condition compel behavior or only reward it?
Can the player refuse?
What authority does another player gain?
How does it clear?
harm_models.best_for: Games that want characters' internal states to generate scenes.
harm_models.risks: Compulsion without consent rules can create player conflict.

harm_models.name: No Formal Harm System
harm_models.description: Injury and danger are handled entirely through fiction, scene authority, or other consequence procedures.
questions: How is lasting harm remembered?
Who determines incapacitation?
What prevents arbitrary severity?
How does recovery become visible?
harm_models.best_for: Games where physical danger is rare, abstract, or outside the main subject.
harm_models.risks: Groups importing expectations from other games may need explicit guidance.

recovery_models.name: Safe Rest
recovery_models.model: Recovery occurs when the character gains genuine safety and enough time.
recovery_models.guidance: Make safety an achieved fictional condition rather than an automatic scene transition.

recovery_models.name: Care from Another
recovery_models.model: Another character's treatment, comfort, or attention clears or reduces harm.
recovery_models.guidance: Use recovery to create relationship scenes, not merely a reset button.

recovery_models.name: Specialist Treatment
recovery_models.model: A qualified person, facility, ritual, or resource is required.
recovery_models.guidance: Establish access, cost, and what treatment cannot restore.

recovery_models.name: Express a Condition
recovery_models.model: The character clears an emotional condition by acting it out or making themselves vulnerable.
recovery_models.guidance: Define the action carefully so it produces meaningful play without forcing unsafe performance.

recovery_models.name: Make Amends
recovery_models.model: Recovery requires addressing harm done to a person or community.
recovery_models.guidance: Do not make forgiveness automatic; the procedure can restore the acting character's integrity without controlling the harmed party.

recovery_models.name: Time Skip
recovery_models.model: A suitable passage of time restores capacity or advances healing.
recovery_models.guidance: Establish what else changes during the skipped time.

recovery_models.name: Resource Spend
recovery_models.model: Supply, currency, favor, or another resource pays for recovery.
recovery_models.guidance: Connect the spend to fictional care or repair when the game's style requires it.

recovery_models.name: Recovery Project
recovery_models.model: Serious harm clears through milestones on a treatment or rehabilitation clock.
recovery_models.guidance: Use milestones to create choices and support rather than repeated identical rolls.

recovery_models.name: Transform Instead of Heal
recovery_models.model: The consequence becomes a lasting trait, scar, new playbook, retirement, or altered relationship.
recovery_models.guidance: Ensure the player understands the stakes before the transformation becomes irreversible.

recovery_models.name: Session Reset
recovery_models.model: Certain short-term states clear at session start or end.
recovery_models.guidance: State exceptions and preserve any fiction that remains relevant.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: Mark Experience on a Miss
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Rewards taking risks and keeps complications from feeling like pure loss.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: End-of-Session Questions
advancement_model_taxonomy.procedure: Players answer thematic questions and mark progress for yes answers.
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Directs attention toward the game's themes and desired session texture.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: Drives, Keys, or Principles
advancement_model_taxonomy.procedure: Advancement follows when a character pursues or resolves defined motivations.
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Makes character priorities visible and rewards thematic commitment.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: Highlighted Stats or Approaches
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Creates rotating incentives but requires clear limits to prevent repetitive rolling.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: Milestone Advancement
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Useful for campaign arcs; define who recognizes a milestone.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: Relationship Resolution
advancement_model_taxonomy.procedure: Changing or resolving bonds grants growth.
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Encourages characters to let relationships evolve rather than preserve optimal bonuses.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: Resource Conversion
advancement_model_taxonomy.procedure: A filled growth, potential, or XP track converts into an advancement.
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Straightforward implementation; state track size and overflow rules.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: Scars or Trauma as Advancement
advancement_model_taxonomy.procedure: Lasting consequences unlock new permissions or changes.
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Power and damage become linked; preserve meaningful player choice around transformation.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: Seasonal or Age Advancement
advancement_model_taxonomy.procedure: Time skips, generations, or campaign phases trigger changes.
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Best for long-timescale games and institutional play.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: Quest or Vow Progress
advancement_model_taxonomy.procedure: Completing progress tracks enables development or legacy changes.
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Advancement follows commitments rather than encounter count.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: Change Playbook
advancement_model_taxonomy.procedure: The character's dramatic role transforms and their rules package changes.
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Provide a migration procedure for retained moves, stats, resources, and relationships.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: Retirement or Legacy
advancement_model_taxonomy.procedure: An advancement exits the character safely or converts them into a setting element.
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Treat retirement as a successful story outcome rather than failure.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: Group, Crew, Family, or Community Advancement
advancement_model_taxonomy.procedure: A shared sheet gains capabilities and changes status.
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Define contribution, ownership, and what happens when characters leave the group.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: Unlock New Scale of Action
advancement_model_taxonomy.procedure: Advancement grants authority over larger institutions, regions, or conflicts.
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Ensure the campaign is ready for the expanded scope.

advancement_model_taxonomy.name: No Persistent Advancement
advancement_model_taxonomy.procedure: The game intentionally avoids cumulative character improvement.
advancement_model_taxonomy.design_use: Use one-shot, episodic, or transformation procedures instead of importing levels.

two_hour_one_shot.scope: One central situation, two or three important NPCs, one major relationship question, and one decisive transformation.
avoid: long lore briefing
more than one major subplot
slow equipment shopping
advancement that cannot matter during the session

four_hour_one_shot.scope: One complete episode with room for relationship scenes, one reversal, and a climax.
four_hour_one_shot.prep: Prepare pressures and questions, not a scene-by-scene script.

six_session_arc.advancement: Choose a pace that allows at least one meaningful character or group change before the final session.
six_session_arc.threat_count: Usually two or three linked pressures are enough.

phases.focus: establish people, rules, relationships, and immediate threats
let factions and consequences reshape the premise
advance transformations, playbook changes, and larger-scale choices
resolve central questions without requiring every thread to close

maintenance: Let characters change playbooks or leave.
Introduce new pressures through consequences, not arbitrary resets.

player_turn_questions: What does my character actually do?
What established facts make this possible or dangerous?
facilitator_response_questions: What do the agenda and principles require?
What result or protection must be honored?
How hard should the move be?
move_resolution_checklist: Confirm game, edition, and move version.
Clarify intent, target, scale, and stakes.
Resolve only with the named randomizer or choice procedure.

algorithm: Confirm the action is possible in the fiction.
Compare the actual description with the move's trigger; do not substitute thematic similarity for the written condition.
Check whether another more specific rule already controls.
Identify whether triggering is mandatory, optional, observed by another participant, or permission-based.
Clarify ambiguous stakes, target, scale, and approach before rolling.
If the trigger is not met, state what happens fictionally or what must change.

resolve_classic_2d6.precondition: Use only when the selected game's move specifies this model.
resolve_classic_2d6.formula: two six-sided dice plus the specified modifier

bands.miss: total 6 or less unless the move says otherwise
bands.weak_hit: total 7–9 unless the move says otherwise
bands.strong_hit: total 10 or more unless the move says otherwise
bands.exceptional: 12+ only when the move or advancement explicitly defines it

algorithm: Add the named modifier and only permitted bonuses or penalties.
Determine the band from the move's current text.
Read and apply the matching result, including every choice and question.
Record forward, ongoing, hold, resources, conditions, or state changes.
Translate the result into fiction before another roll.
Load the exact procedure named by the game.
Validate that all inputs and fictional prerequisites exist.
Generate or choose the result exactly as instructed.
Assign choices and narration to the named authorities.
Apply outputs atomically when possible so no granted benefit is forgotten.
Return a record of fictional and mechanical changes.

procedure: List every plausible triggered rule.
Remove rules whose fictional conditions are not actually met.
Use explicit priority text if present.
Resolve the first rule whose outcome can determine whether later triggers still exist.
Avoid charging the same cost twice unless the rules explicitly create separate consequences.
After each resolution, reevaluate the fiction rather than assuming the remaining moves still trigger.
Hold the dice or pause resolution.
Each participant states what part of the trigger or result does not land.
Check the exact current wording and examples.
Identify the move's underlying purpose and what promise it makes.
Agree on strict application, a transparent accommodation, or a different fictional approach.
Do not secretly downgrade a result after the roll.

character.warning: A storage superset for software. A specific game will use only some fields and may require different ones.

mechanical_fields.ratings: Map of stats, labels, approaches, or other values.
mechanical_fields.moves: References to basic, playbook, custom, peripheral, and temporary moves.
mechanical_fields.resources: Typed current/maximum records with source and refresh rules.
mechanical_fields.conditions: Named or freeform state records with effects and clearing instructions.
mechanical_fields.harm: One or more game-specific harm models.
mechanical_fields.relationships: Directional or mutual records such as Hx, bonds, strings, debts, influence, or history.
mechanical_fields.equipment: Items, tags, uses, load, quality, damage state, range, permissions, and ownership.
mechanical_fields.advancement: Experience tracks, marked questions, chosen improvements, repeat limits, and playbook changes.
mechanical_fields.powers: Game-specific techniques, spells, assets, forms, rituals, or permissions.
mechanical_fields.clocks: Personal progress, danger, transformation, or recovery tracks.

validation_rules: Do not require a stat array if the game has no stats.
Relationship values must identify direction unless the game explicitly makes them mutual.
Every resource must include its source and refresh or removal rule.
Every condition should link to its mechanical effect and clearing procedure when those exist.
A move reference must include game and version to prevent same-name collisions.
Player identity fields and safety preferences must not be exposed publicly without consent.

implementation_safety: Store exact proprietary text only when the user has rights or the material's license permits it.
Keep paraphrased teaching summaries separate from authoritative rules text.
Version moves because titles and triggers can change between editions.
Never infer a trigger from the move name alone.
Do not allow a generic engine to invent a miss result when the move specifies one.

validation_rules: Game and version must be explicit.
Safety fields are private by default and editable without in-fiction cost.
Threats and countdowns record current state, not predetermined protagonist choices.
Session summaries distinguish confirmed facts from open questions and facilitator-only prep.
Custom rules include author, date, purpose, and rollback instructions.

move_integrity: duration and scale explicit when needed
state_integrity: resource changes cannot exceed defined bounds unless overflow rule exists
directional relationships keep source and target
condition clearing never occurs without its procedure
safety: pause and veto actions never consume in-fiction resources
PvP automation requires table policy and player confirmation
copyright: exact source text must have license or permission metadata
commercial move lists excluded by default

rules_loader_priority: load official errata and play materials
load this database's generic teaching support only where no conflict exists

prep_philosophy: Prepare active pressures, not a sequence of required scenes.
Prepare what important people and forces want, what they can do, and what happens if no one intervenes.
Leave blank space for answers created by playbooks and player questions.
Use the game's exact prep structures before generic templates.
Revise preparation after every material player success; preparation is not protected from play.

campaign_arc: questions that cannot be answered in advance

portrayal_rules: Give the NPC a concrete desire and a capacity to act.
Do not reduce every NPC to a clue dispenser or combat obstacle.
Let NPCs change when protagonists provide new reasons.
Distinguish what the facilitator knows from what the NPC knows.
Keep mechanics only where the specific game requires them.

action_cycle: Choose the faction whose goal has the clearest opportunity.
Advance it according to resources and methods.
Show a sign before severe irreversible change when the game's hardness allows.
Update affected relationships, locations, and clocks.
Do not act every faction every session; prioritize what touches the protagonists.

questions: What can characters do here that is difficult elsewhere?
What pressure becomes visible on arrival?
Who will notice change?
What image should recur when the place returns?
What would make the place permanently different?

advance_rules: Advance only from an established trigger, facilitator move, project result, or passage of relevant time.
Apply the stage effect when crossed; do not tick silently if visibility matters.
Pause, reduce, replace, or delete the clock after effective intervention.
Do not use a clock to force an outcome the protagonists have already prevented.
Expose enough information for players to make meaningful decisions unless secrecy is itself part of the game's procedure.

procedure: Select one consequence or opportunity directly connected to prior choices.
Frame a concrete place and moment rather than summarizing abstract history.
Put at least one protagonist in position to act immediately.
Ask a question whose answer matters now.
Use a previously established NPC, promise, injury, resource, or image when possible.

session_end_audit: Resolve the game's end-of-session move or questions.
Mark experience, growth, recovery, relationships, and shared resources.
Record facts established by moves and answers.
Update threats, countdowns, factions, and locations changed by play.
List unresolved promises and choices without deciding their outcomes.
Check whether any player needs debrief, aftercare, or a private follow-up.
Confirm next-session logistics separately from in-fiction epilogues.

stalled_scene: Ask what each character wants right now.
Show a sign of an approaching threat.
Offer an opportunity with a cost.
Cut to another character or advance time.
players_ignore_prep: Reinterpret prepared NPCs and threats according to their motives rather than their intended scene.
Let unattended pressures act offscreen when justified.
Discard preparation that no longer matters.
unexpected_strong_hit: Ask the player what success looks like.
Create new responsibility from the changed world rather than negating the win.
rules_uncertainty: Pause and identify the exact move.
Do not punish a player for relying on the ruling.

methods: Ask the character whose decision is most urgent.
Cut when a result directly affects another protagonist.
Pause one scene at a decision and visit another unresolved pressure.
Invite a quieter player with a concrete question rather than a vague demand to participate.
Return to a character after enough fictional time has passed for their action to matter.
Use playbook authority to decide who answers a setting or relationship question.
warning_signs: one player makes most group decisions
the same character triggers every information move
offscreen characters receive no consequences or opportunities
cuts repeatedly occur before one player's choices resolve
spotlight_management.audit_rule: Spotlight quality is measured by meaningful decisions and consequences, not equal speaking time alone.

hard: separate or capture after an exposed action
make an irreversible change authorized by the rules
checks: Did a move grant this authority?

signs_of_pressure: a familiar person in the wrong place
scene_turns: the ally asks for something unacceptable
the missing resource was deliberately withheld
the threat's goal is understandable but harmful
the safest route requires betraying a value

move_pattern_catalog.scope: Original generic patterns for teaching and design. None are official or universal moves.

patterns.name: Face Immediate Peril
patterns.design_purpose: Resolve immediate peril where hesitation, exposure, or force can materially change who controls the situation.
patterns.fictional_trigger: When you act despite a present, clearly described danger that can strike before you finish.
trigger_questions: Has the described fictional action actually happened or been committed to?
Is the named pressure, uncertainty, or relationship present in the established fiction?
Does the chosen game's real move already cover this situation more specifically?
What outcome is the character trying to secure, and what can oppose or complicate it?
fictional_prerequisites: The action is possible at the established scale.
The character has the access, position, tools, permission, or relationship required by the fiction.
The result can produce a meaningful change rather than a cosmetic answer.

classic_2d6_example_model.use_note: Illustrative only. A real game may use other dice, cards, tokens, automatic choices, or no randomizer.
classic_2d6_example_model.roll: 2d6 plus the stat or modifier selected by the specific game
classic_2d6_example_model.strong_hit_shape: The character gains the stated objective and keeps meaningful control of the follow-through.
classic_2d6_example_model.weak_hit_shape: The objective is gained incompletely or at a cost; the player normally chooses or accepts a concrete complication.
classic_2d6_example_model.miss_shape: The danger acts decisively, the situation escalates, or the GM makes a move grounded in the established threat.
classic_2d6_example_model.twelve_plus_option: A game may add an exceptional result, but 12+ is not universally special.

result_design_checklist: Promise a concrete fictional outcome rather than only a numerical bonus.
Ensure every listed choice can matter immediately.
Do not make the mixed result secretly worse than the miss.
On a miss, make a consequence that follows from the established threat or opportunity.
State who chooses each option and who answers each question.
Define duration, scale, targets, and resource costs when ambiguity would produce conflict.
facilitator_follow_through: Restate what changed in the fiction.
Honor every protection, answer, choice, or permission the result grants.
Show the new danger, opening, cost, or relationship consequence.
Shift the spotlight when another character is immediately affected.
Ask what the acting character does next only after the result is fully applied.
common_misuses: Calling for the move because the task feels difficult even though the trigger is absent.
Allowing a roll to bypass fictional requirements the character has not met.
Treating a weak hit as no progress.
Using a miss to negate facts already established or to punish the player arbitrarily.
Resolving the number but failing to narrate a changed situation.

facilitator_follow_through: Restate what changed in the fiction.

Treating a weak hit as no progress.
Using a miss to negate facts already established or to punish the player arbitrarily.
Resolving the number but failing to narrate a changed situation.

classic_2d6_example_model.use_note: Illustrative only. A real game may use other dice, cards, tokens, automatic choices, or no randomizer.
classic_2d6_example_model.roll: 2d6 plus the stat or modifier selected by the specific game
classic_2d6_example_model.strong_hit_shape: The procedure establishes a strong, usable scene fact or transition and gives the acting player meaningful authorship.
classic_2d6_example_model.weak_hit_shape: The transition succeeds but includes a limitation, unresolved question, or cost that shapes the next scene.
classic_2d6_example_model.miss_shape: The next scene begins under pressure, with an unwanted truth, or after the opposition has acted.
classic_2d6_example_model.twelve_plus_option: A game may add an exceptional result, but 12+ is not universally special.

result_design_checklist: Promise a concrete fictional outcome rather than only a numerical bonus.
Ensure every listed choice can matter immediately.
Do not make the mixed result secretly worse than the miss.
On a miss, make a consequence that follows from the established threat or opportunity.
State who chooses each option and who answers each question.
Define duration, scale, targets, and resource costs when ambiguity would produce conflict.
facilitator_follow_through: Restate what changed in the fiction.
Honor every protection, answer, choice, or permission the result grants.
Show the new danger, opening, cost, or relationship consequence.
Shift the spotlight when another character is immediately affected.
Ask what the acting character does next only after the result is fully applied.
common_misuses: Calling for the move because the task feels difficult even though the trigger is absent.
Allowing a roll to bypass fictional requirements the character has not met.
Treating a weak hit as no progress.
Using a miss to negate facts already established or to punish the player arbitrarily.
Resolving the number but failing to narrate a changed situation.

playbook_archetype_pattern_catalog.scope: Original dramatic-role patterns for design and analysis; not playable official playbooks.

patterns.name: The Protector
patterns.central_question: Who are you unable to abandon, and what does protection cost them?
character_creation_prompts: What event made you the protector rather than merely someone with similar skills?
Which other protagonist has seen the part of you that contradicts this archetype?
What do you want right now that the archetype's expected role makes difficult?
Which institution, community, person, or force benefits when you remain in this role?
What visible detail tells the table when this tension is active?
move_design_targets: Create at least one move that rewards engaging the central tension rather than avoiding it.
Give the playbook a distinctive permission or question, not only a larger modifier.
Include a cost or vulnerability that produces play without making the character unusable.
Connect at least one move to another protagonist or a shared setting element.
Ensure advancement can transform the archetype rather than only intensify it.
relationship_prompts: Who expects you to perform this role?
Who gives you permission to be different?
Who has paid for your past choices?
Whose judgment matters more than you admit?
advancement_directions: resolve or transform the central tension
retire, transcend, or replace the playbook when supported by the game
patterns.warning: An archetype is not a personality prescription. The player retains authority over the protagonist except where the chosen game's rules explicitly allocate it.

worked_examples.scope: Original examples showing trigger analysis and fiction-mechanics-fiction follow-through.

examples.title: Worked example: Face Immediate Peril
examples.fictional_setup: The scene takes place in a collapsing elevated walkway above a crowded market.
examples.player_intent: The character wants to reach a trapped worker before the supports fail.
examples.established_pressure: The structure, distance, and falling debris are already established.
examples.player_description: The player describes a concrete approach that could trigger Face Immediate Peril; they do not merely announce a move name.

trigger_analysis.likely_trigger: When you act despite a present, clearly described danger that can strike before you finish.
questions_to_confirm: Has the described fictional action actually happened or been committed to?
Is the named pressure, uncertainty, or relationship present in the established fiction?
Does the chosen game's real move already cover this situation more specifically?
trigger_analysis.no_roll_case: If the pressure is absent or the approach automatically achieves the intent, narrate the result without forcing a move.
trigger_analysis.impossible_case: If the established fiction denies the required access or scale, explain what must change before the move can trigger.

illustrative_resolution.strong_hit: The character gains the stated objective and keeps meaningful control of the follow-through. The facilitator asks the player to describe the visible sign of that control.
illustrative_resolution.weak_hit: The objective is gained incompletely or at a cost; the player normally chooses or accepts a concrete complication. The chosen cost becomes true immediately and opens the next decision.
illustrative_resolution.miss: The danger acts decisively, the situation escalates, or the GM makes a move grounded in the established threat. The facilitator does not erase the attempt; the attempt becomes part of why the situation changes.

follow_through_sequence: State the mechanical result and choices.
Translate every choice into concrete fictional change.
Update resources, conditions, relationships, clocks, or position.
Show who notices or is affected.
Move the spotlight or ask what happens next.
examples.common_wrong_resolution: Roll, announce the numerical band, and return to the unchanged scene.
examples.corrective_principle: A resolved move is incomplete until the shared fiction has changed.

original_guide_examples.label: No move is needed
original_guide_examples.fiction: The character has the office key, no one is watching, and nothing is pressuring them.
original_guide_examples.player_statement: I unlock the office and go inside.
original_guide_examples.resolution: The door opens. The GM describes what is inside. No roll is created merely because entering could lead to future trouble.
original_guide_examples.lesson: Moves resolve the situations they are designed for; they are not universal permission checks.

original_guide_examples.label: Original illustrative danger move
original_guide_examples.copyright_status: Original example written for this guide; not a published move.

sample_move.trigger: When you cross unstable ground while immediate danger closes in, roll +Nerve.
sample_move.10_plus: You get across and choose one advantage: keep your gear secure, bring someone with you, or reach a superior position.
sample_move.7_to_9: You get across, but choose one: leave something behind, arrive exposed, or allow the danger to advance.
sample_move.miss: The GM makes an appropriate move based on the collapsing route and approaching threat.

original_guide_examples.fiction: A character runs across a failing catwalk while security drones close in.
original_guide_examples.result: The player gets across and chooses to leave a heavy equipment case behind.
original_guide_examples.follow_through: The GM describes the case crashing into the machinery below and asks the next character whether they jump now or grab the case.
original_guide_examples.lesson: A 7-9 advances the character's goal and the danger at the same time.

original_guide_examples.label: A miss need not mean incompetence
original_guide_examples.fiction: A highly trained hunter examines a perfect crime scene while the culprit monitors the building.
original_guide_examples.poor_interpretation: The expert suddenly cannot recognize obvious evidence.
original_guide_examples.better_interpretation: The expert finds the evidence, but the culprit realizes exactly what they found and cuts power to the building.
original_guide_examples.lesson: Consequences can arise from opposition and changing circumstances rather than personal failure.

original_guide_examples.label: Fictional leverage before a social move
original_guide_examples.fiction: A character demands that a hostile official release a prisoner but offers no reason, threat, evidence, authority, or bargain.
original_guide_examples.resolution: The GM explains that the official has no reason to comply and asks what leverage the character creates.
original_guide_examples.next_action: The character reveals proof that the official's superior ordered the release.
original_guide_examples.move_check: Now the chosen game's manipulation or persuasion procedure may apply.
original_guide_examples.lesson: A high social stat does not automatically replace the fictional requirements of a move.

original_guide_examples.label: Combat is about fictional objectives
original_guide_examples.fiction: A character fires across a warehouse to stop a guard from reaching an alarm.
original_guide_examples.clarification: The goal is not simply to reduce the guard's hit points; it is to control movement before the alarm is triggered.
original_guide_examples.resolution: Use the move that matches suppressing, attacking, protecting, or acting under pressure in the chosen game.
original_guide_examples.follow_through: Apply the move's exact harm, position, or choice result and decide whether the alarm remains reachable.
original_guide_examples.lesson: The move follows intent, method, and situation, not a universal attack action.

original_guide_examples.label: Honor a strong hit
original_guide_examples.fiction: A move promises that on 10+ the character escapes cleanly.
original_guide_examples.incorrect_gm_response: You escape, but the enemy secretly tagged your vehicle and stole your supplies.
original_guide_examples.correct_gm_response: The character escapes cleanly. The GM advances unrelated off-screen events only if another rule authorizes it and it does not undermine the promised result.
original_guide_examples.lesson: Do not smuggle a mixed-result cost into a strong hit.

original_guide_examples.label: Pause when a move does not land
original_guide_examples.fiction: A player chooses an option that another participant cannot reconcile with the established scale of the scene.
procedure: Pause.
Restate the move's promise.
Explain the fictional conflict.
Brainstorm an interpretation or mutually accepted adjustment.
Return to the written option if no adjustment is agreed.
Resume only after everyone understands what is now true.
original_guide_examples.lesson: The move text is the baseline of the table's agreement, not a weapon for overruling communication.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Treating PbtA as one universal 2d6 system
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Identify the exact game and use its native rules.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Rolling whenever an action is uncertain
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Ask whether a move or specific procedure applies. If not, resolve through fiction.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Calling a move by name without describing the action
