common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Clarify what the character actually does and wants.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Treating 7-9 as failure
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Apply the move's hit, then its cost, reduced effect, choice, or complication.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Making a miss mean 'nothing happens'
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Advance a threat, reveal something, inflict an established cost, or use the move's miss text.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Making every miss humiliating
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Let opposition, scarcity, timing, collateral danger, or external events create the consequence.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Using the same generic complication for every 7-9
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Read and apply the exact move.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Ignoring fictional position because the modifier is high
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Determine permission, trigger, scope, and effect before rolling.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Adding tactical turns and NPC attack rolls by habit
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Use spotlight and GM moves unless the game specifies a battle sequence.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Prewriting a plot
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Prepare threats, motives, places, and consequences, then play to find out.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Hiding all danger until after the roll
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Telegraph risks when the characters could reasonably perceive them.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Weakening a strong hit to preserve challenge
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Honor the result and make the next problem emerge honestly from the changed fiction.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Announcing GM move names
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Describe what happens in the world.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Assuming playbooks must be balanced like combat classes
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Evaluate spotlight, thematic authority, and narrative pressure, not only damage output.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Letting one character trigger every scene
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Cut the spotlight and ask other characters what they do.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Ignoring end-of-session procedures
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Reserve time for experience, relationship changes, recovery, and reflection.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Using 'fiction first' as permission to ignore rules
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Let fiction trigger rules and let rules change fiction; neither side erases the other.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Assuming the GM may control a player character's feelings or decisions
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Follow the exact authority granted by the move and use consent and disagreement procedures.

ten_minute_orientation: Name the exact game and premise.
Explain that players describe actions before choosing dice.
Show the result bands or procedure actually used.
Explain what a weak hit and miss mean in this game.
Point out the sheet's harm, condition, relationship, and advancement records.
Begin play and teach remaining rules at the first trigger.
traditional_rpg_player: Replace 'What skill do I roll?' with 'What does your character do?'
Explain that difficulty is often fictional rather than a changing target number.
Show that a mixed result is progress with consequence.
Explain that the facilitator's chapter contains binding procedures.
new_facilitator: Read agenda, principles, and moves aloud or summarize them visibly.
Prepare one pressure and several questions.
Practice soft versus hard versions of the same move.
After each roll, say what changes before asking for another.
software_developer: Model games and move versions separately.
Do not hard-code 2d6 or universal result bands.
Treat fiction prerequisites as first-class data.
Keep licensed exact text separate from original summaries.

traditional_to_pbta_conversion.principle: Convert fictional identity and dramatic function before numbers. Select a specific target PbtA game; there is no system-neutral finished character conversion.

workflow.name: Choose the target game
workflow.instruction: Match premise, tone, campaign scale, facilitator model, and recurring activities.

workflow.name: Extract the concept
workflow.instruction: Write what the character does, wants, fears, protects, and changes in others without rules terminology.

workflow.name: Identify signature permissions
workflow.instruction: List extraordinary things the character can do in the fiction, including scale, tools, knowledge, and social access.

workflow.name: Identify dramatic tensions
workflow.instruction: Choose the two or three unresolved pressures that should generate scenes.

workflow.name: Choose a playbook or framework
workflow.instruction: Select the closest dramatic role, not merely the closest combat class.

workflow.name: Rebuild relationships
workflow.instruction: Answer the target game's relationship questions using the old campaign only as inspiration.

workflow.name: Translate gear and powers
workflow.instruction: Keep iconic items and abilities as tags, permissions, moves, assets, or techniques appropriate to the new game.

workflow.name: Set campaign state
workflow.instruction: Convert factions, locations, threats, and obligations into the target game's prep structures.

workflow.name: Discard incompatible math
workflow.instruction: Do not preserve armor class, exact hit points, challenge ratings, spell-slot counts, proficiency bonuses, or level-by-level parity unless the target game explicitly has equivalents.

workflow.name: Playtest the identity
workflow.instruction: After one session, revise any option that fails to produce the intended fictional role.

concept_mapping.class: playbook or archetype only when the dramatic role matches
concept_mapping.level: campaign history, selected advancements, scale of permissions, or no direct equivalent
concept_mapping.ability_score: target game's stat, label, approach, or no direct equivalent
concept_mapping.skill_proficiency: fictional background, permission, move, specialty, or question authority
concept_mapping.armor_class: fictional defense, armor tag, harm reduction, move effect, or no equivalent
concept_mapping.hit_points: harm clock, conditions, stress, injuries, durability, or no equivalent
concept_mapping.spell: move, asset, technique, ritual, permission, resource spend, or fictional capability
concept_mapping.spell_slot: charges, fatigue, hold, stress, preparation requirement, cost choice, or no equivalent
concept_mapping.feat: playbook move, advancement, asset, tag, or custom move
concept_mapping.alignment: drive, principle, belief, question, relationship pressure, or omitted
concept_mapping.initiative: spotlight procedure, exchange system, or no direct equivalent
concept_mapping.challenge_rating: threat impulse, permissions, scale, harm, countdown, and fictional capability

traditional_to_pbta_conversion.warning: A direct numerical conversion usually produces a character that fits neither game's incentives.

move_design_workflow.name: Name the recurring fictional moment
move_design_workflow.test: Would this situation appear often enough to deserve procedure?

move_design_workflow.name: Define the trigger
move_design_workflow.test: Can the table recognize when it occurs without reading the designer's mind?

move_design_workflow.name: Name the game's purpose
move_design_workflow.test: What theme, dilemma, authority, or momentum should the move create?

move_design_workflow.name: Choose resolution mode
move_design_workflow.test: Would automatic effect, choice, resource spend, questions, cards, or dice express it best?

move_design_workflow.name: Draft every result
move_design_workflow.test: Does each result change the fiction and preserve the game's subject?

move_design_workflow.name: Assign authority
move_design_workflow.test: Who rolls, chooses, answers, and narrates each part?

move_design_workflow.name: Set scale and duration
move_design_workflow.test: What can the result affect and when does it end?

move_design_workflow.name: Test edge cases
move_design_workflow.test: What happens in PvP, group action, repeated use, impossible action, or overlapping triggers?

move_design_workflow.name: Playtest
move_design_workflow.test: Do players pursue the intended fiction rather than only the best modifier?

move_design_workflow.name: Revise and version
move_design_workflow.test: Can users identify which text is current and migrate old records?

dimensions.trigger_clarity: 0 absent; 1 vague theme; 2 recognizable action; 3 precise fictional condition with edge guidance
dimensions.fictional_relevance: 0 arbitrary; 1 decorative; 2 changes situation; 3 directly expresses premise or theme
dimensions.result_integrity: 0 dead result; 1 numerical only; 2 actionable changes; 3 each band creates distinct meaningful momentum
dimensions.authority_clarity: 0 unknown; 1 inferred; 2 chooser identified; 3 all questions, choices, and narration allocated
dimensions.mixed_result_quality: 0 disguised failure; 1 generic cost; 2 meaningful tradeoff; 3 several genre-specific pressures
dimensions.miss_quality: 0 nothing happens; 1 arbitrary punishment; 2 grounded escalation; 3 grounded escalation that creates future choices
dimensions.implementation_completeness: 0 unusable; 1 missing fields; 2 functional; 3 versioned, testable, and auditable

interpretation.19-21: strong draft; still requires table testing

compatibility_workflow: Identify source and target game editions.
Compare authority allocation and facilitator model.
Compare harm, relationships, resources, and advancement.
Translate fictional purpose rather than wording or numbers.
Rewrite triggers and results in the target game's vocabulary.
Test interactions with every basic move and end-state.
Label the conversion as custom material and version it.
copyright_safe_design_practice: Study how a rule allocates authority and shapes play.
Write new wording from the intended fictional problem.
Do not reconstruct a commercial playbook by paraphrasing every field in order.
Use licensed SRDs only within their actual scope and conditions.
Credit inspirations even when permission is not legally required.
Keep provenance for every imported exact text fragment.

terms.definition: Powered by the Apocalypse; a self-applied family label for games inspired by Apocalypse World or by other PbtA games, not a universal engine specification.
The game by Meguey Baker and D. Vincent Baker that originated the PbtA publishing and design lineage.
The shared exchange of description, questions, decisions, rules, and consequences through which play occurs.
The currently established imagined facts: people, places, actions, relationships, objects, risks, and events.
Begin with what happens in the fiction and use mechanics when the game's procedures are triggered; it does not mean mechanics are optional.
Fiction triggers or constrains a rule; the rule produces an outcome; the outcome becomes new fiction.
A rule that structures a specific part of the conversation, often with a trigger and outcome procedure.
A move broadly available to protagonists in a game that uses that category.
A move supplied by or selected through a particular character framework.
A move for a specialized recurring procedure outside the central basic-move set.
A move created for a specific threat, location, item, situation, campaign, or adaptation.
An instruction or option telling the facilitator how to change or respond to the fiction.
The fictional or procedural condition that brings a move into effect.
A trigger that requires resolving the move when its conditions occur.
A rule the player may choose to invoke rather than one that automatically triggers.
A procedure activated by permission, timing, or choice rather than a conventional fictional when-clause.
The favorable high result band in many PbtA games; its exact threshold and effect are game-specific.
A favorable but complicated middle result band in many PbtA games, often called a 7–9 in classic 2d6 designs.
A result combining progress with cost, danger, reduced effect, or choice; not every PbtA game uses this term or structure.
A low result that gives the game permission to change or escalate the situation according to its rules; not necessarily character incompetence.
An exceptional high result used by some moves or advancement rules; it is not universal.
Add a character value to a randomizer result, commonly but not necessarily 2d6.
A rated quality used by a game's procedures; it may represent capability, approach, emotion, identity, or relationship.
A stat-like descriptor whose value can shift as characters' self-image or others' influence changes.
A rated method or attitude used to resolve actions in some games.
A temporary bonus or permission applying to the next qualifying action or roll.
A continuing modifier or permission while its stated condition remains true.
A quantity granted by a move and spent later only for the options that move allows.
Increase a roll or value by one under the granting rule; stacking and duration are game-specific.
Decrease a roll or value by one under the granting rule; stacking and duration are game-specific.
The permissions and constraints created by location, approach, scale, leverage, equipment, relationships, and established facts.
A rule or fictional fact establishing that a character may attempt or accomplish something.
What an action can accomplish at the established scale.
How exposed, controlled, or dangerous an attempted action is; explicit position ratings are characteristic of some descendants, not all PbtA games.
A fictional reason another person might listen, bargain, or change behavior.
The right and responsibility to answer a category of question or establish a category of fact.
A broad informal term for who can establish fictional facts; a game's actual authority is usually divided by specific procedures.
A roll made by a player while the facilitator responds without an opposed roll.
A structure without one permanent traditional facilitator; authority is distributed through procedures.
A mode in which players share world and opposition duties according to the game's rules.
Play by one person using oracles, prompts, procedures, and interpretation to distribute uncertainty.
Master of Ceremonies, the facilitator title used by Apocalypse World and some related games.
A facilitator title used by some mystery and monster-hunting PbtA games.
The facilitator's highest-level goals for how to conduct play.
A decision-making rule guiding description, preparation, and facilitator moves.
A rule limiting the sources from which a facilitator's statements should come, such as honesty, preparation, and rules.
Prepare active pressures and honest situations without deciding the protagonists' choices or final outcome in advance.

terms.term: ask questions and use the answers
terms.definition: Invite players to establish relevant fiction, then treat their answers as consequential facts rather than decorative suggestions.
Apocalypse World's vivid instruction to describe the world through concrete, charged, genre-specific details.
A facilitator move that warns, foreshadows, or presents danger while leaving clear room to respond.
A facilitator move that applies an established consequence decisively when authorized by the rules and fiction.
The immediacy and severity with which a facilitator move changes the situation.
A clear fictional opening for a facilitator consequence, often after ignored danger or unprotected action.
The table's current attention and decision space focused on a particular character or situation.
Deliberately sharing attention, cutting between simultaneous pressures, and inviting quieter players.
A character framework combining identity, thematic tension, permissions, moves, relationships, resources, and advancement.
A recognizable dramatic role used to organize a playbook without fully defining the character's personality.
A short set of appearance choices or prompts used to make a character immediately concrete.
A motivation that may guide play or trigger experience.
A paired or ordered set of beliefs whose position changes through play in some games.
History, a directional relationship rating in Apocalypse World; similar abbreviations are not universal.
A relationship statement or resource whose exact operation depends on the game.
A token of emotional leverage used by some relationship-focused games.
A tracked social obligation recognized by people or factions in some games.
Mechanical authority over another character's self-image or choices within explicit limits.
A shared resource representing coordination or support in some games.
A scarce resource used to avoid, alter, or survive outcomes in some games.
A resource representing pressure or exertion, often spent to push, resist, or activate capabilities.
A banked advantage resource used by some PbtA games, especially Ironsworn.
A named state with fictional and mechanical effects, often cleared by specific actions.
A game-specific representation of injury, damage, or dangerous consequence.
A game-specific protection that may reduce harm or establish fictional resistance.
A harm-related state in some games; it has no universal definition.
A procedure governing recovery; its trigger and effects are game-specific.
A segmented tracker for progress, danger, escalation, opportunity, or a changing state.
An ordered sequence showing how a threat escalates if nothing changes it.
A preparation structure grouping dangers, stakes, and impending outcomes in some games.
An active person, force, institution, scarcity, location, or condition with an impulse and capacity to act.
A prepared source of pressure, especially in Dungeon World-style fronts; terminology varies.
A structured scenario involving questions, clues, threats, and resolution procedures.
A prepared or emergent sequence of pressures spanning sessions.
An organized group with goals, resources, methods, relationships, and the ability to act.
A non-player character portrayed according to the game's authority structure.
A player character or protagonist controlled primarily by a player.
Player-versus-player conflict; a game's rules and table agreement must define consent and authority.
A player's real-world agreement to participate; no in-fiction leverage or move overrides it.
Content excluded from play.
Content that may exist but is not described directly or in detail.
A table procedure allowing anyone to stop play and address safety, clarity, or comfort.
The agreement that participants may step away or leave without punishment or required explanation.
Emotional spillover between player and character experience; not a rules requirement and should be handled carefully.
A pre-play conversation for premise, expectations, characters, safety, logistics, and rules.
The opening play session, often supported by special questions and low-prep procedures.
A complete game experience intended for one session or a very short fixed run.
Connected sessions in which consequences, relationships, threats, and characters persist.
A procedure resolving growth, questions, resources, relationships, or campaign state after play.
A rule that changes a character, group, or setting after earned progress.
A tracked resource or mark used for advancement in some games.
An advancement track often associated with learning through misses in some games.
A development resource or advancement process used by some games.
An advancement or transformation that moves a character into a different dramatic framework.
A procedure for ending a character's active protagonist role, often as a successful outcome.
Play spanning generations, institutions, or replacement protagonists.
A random or structured prompt that answers questions when no human facilitator holds that authority.
A move whose effectiveness depends on previously marked progress rather than a normal stat alone.
A modular capability card or package used by some games instead of a class playbook.
Several dice rolled together and interpreted by a selection rule, such as taking the highest.
A procedure from Blades in the Dark for rating risk and impact before a roll; not a universal PbtA rule.
A procedure that reduces or avoids a consequence at a cost in some games.
A procedure establishing prior preparation during the current action, often with a cost based on improbability or complexity.
Structured activity between major actions, missions, episodes, or adventures.
A focused criminal operation in Blades in the Dark; not a generic synonym for every PbtA mission.
A descriptive quality that grants permissions or constraints through the fiction or explicit tag rules.
A concise rules-bearing descriptor attached to gear, characters, threats, or conditions.
A descriptor indicating the fictional distance at which an item or effect operates.
An effect applying to a group or region; exact targeting is game-specific.
A gear or harm tag in some games suggesting especially destructive or gruesome consequences.
A tag in some games indicating knockback or strong positional impact.
A lasting impairment tracked separately from ordinary harm in some games.
A selected advancement option.
The list of improvements available to a character or group.
A conditional package of new moves entered through fiction in Dungeon World and related designs.
A new or modified character framework created for a particular game.
An informal term for a game or modification derived from another design; use attribution and licensing correctly.
Changing how a game plays through interpretation or house rules without fully redesigning its text.
Adapting characters, setting, or campaign material between games; mechanics usually require redesign rather than direct translation.
The degree to which procedures and content can be used together without contradiction; PbtA games are not automatically compatible.
System Reference Document, a publisher-provided rules reference whose license and scope must be checked individually.
A sheet, card, menu, or reference summarizing procedures for use at the table.
The literal published procedure, used as the stable baseline for resolving disagreement.
A claimed design purpose; prefer official clarification over speculation.
A temporary interpretation made to continue play, later reviewed against the game's text if needed.
A discussed exception or adjustment when a rule's strict application does not land, while preserving its purpose and table agreement.
The range of fictional variation a move can handle without losing its intended structure.
The way one move's result changes the fiction and naturally creates the conditions for later moves.
An informal phrase for consequences that continue play; not a universal rule and not always equivalent to PbtA miss design.
An informal description of some weak hits; exact move text determines the result.
Designing rules so recurring choices and consequences produce a specific genre's patterns.
A question, tension, value, or idea repeatedly explored through procedures and fiction.
The specific kind of protagonists, situation, conflict, and activity the game is built to support.
The scale and subject matter a rule or game is designed to handle.
The emotional and stylistic quality of play, established through rules and table agreement.
What can meaningfully change because of a choice or result.
A fictional or mechanical change following from action, danger, or procedure.
A resource, risk, obligation, limitation, or change accepted for progress.
How a rule structures available options, who chooses, and what each choice means.
A range of outcomes mapped to a roll total or other randomizer result.
Dice, cards, tokens, tables, or another uncertainty mechanism.
A procedure resolved through automatic effect, choice, resource spend, comparison, or authority rather than dice.
A list of choices granted by a move result.
A set of options from which a player or facilitator selects a stated number.
A move that grants specific questions and requires truthful answers.
The promise that a move's granted answer is accurate and useful within its wording.
The size, duration, reach, and magnitude of what an action can affect.
A moment when a result directly creates a question or danger for another character.
A software or design model representing play as transitions among defined states.
The order used when a game-specific rule, general guidance, table agreement, or reference conflicts.
A field warning that the procedure is an example or taxonomy item, not shared by all PbtA games.

questions.question: Is Powered by the Apocalypse one game system?
questions.answer: No. It is a self-applied family label for games inspired by Apocalypse World or other PbtA games. Always begin with the specific game's rules.

questions.question: What is the latest edition of PbtA?
questions.answer: There is no universal PbtA edition. As of July 28, 2026, Apocalypse World Third Edition had preview material, while Apocalypse World Second Edition remained the stable complete classic reference used by this database.

questions.question: Do all PbtA games use 2d6?
questions.answer: No. Many do, but others use dice pools, action dice against challenge dice, cards, tokens, comparisons, or no randomizer.

questions.question: Do all PbtA games use 10+, 7–9, and 6-?
questions.answer: No. Those are classic result bands, not a family requirement.

questions.question: Who decides when a move triggers?
questions.answer: Use the game's text and authority rules. Usually the table compares the described fiction with the trigger, with the facilitator clarifying ambiguities.

questions.question: Can I just say the move name?
questions.answer: You can name it for clarity, but the table still needs to know what the character actually does and how the trigger is met.

questions.question: Can the GM call for a generic check?
questions.answer: Only if the specific game provides one. Uncertainty alone does not create a universal PbtA roll.

questions.question: What happens when no move triggers?
questions.answer: Follow the established fiction: the action may happen, be impossible, require more positioning, or prompt a facilitator response.

questions.question: Does a 7–9 mean failure?
questions.answer: Usually it is a hit with a complication, cost, reduced effect, or hard choice, but the exact move text controls.

questions.question: Does a miss mean nothing happens?
questions.answer: No. A miss normally gives the game permission to make a consequential response; sometimes a move defines a specific miss result.

questions.question: Can a miss still accomplish the task?
questions.answer: Yes, if the move or facilitator consequence makes success-with-severe-consequence appropriate. A miss does not universally negate the character's intent.

questions.question: Does the GM roll dice?
questions.answer: Often not, but some games give the facilitator rolls or other random procedures. Follow the specific game.

questions.question: Is combat a separate minigame?
questions.answer: Often no; many PbtA games use the normal conversation and moves. Some, such as Avatar Legends, add a distinct structured exchange procedure.

questions.question: Is there initiative?
questions.answer: Not universally. Spotlight often follows the fiction, but some games provide turn or exchange procedures.

questions.question: Do NPCs have full player-character sheets?
questions.answer: Usually not, but the game's NPC rules determine what they need.

questions.question: Can players oppose one another?
questions.answer: Only within the game's PvP rules and the group's consent agreement. A move never overrides real-world consent.

questions.question: Can influence or strings control another player character?
questions.answer: Only to the exact extent stated by the game and agreed at the table; they are not permission to coerce a player.

questions.question: Are playbooks classes?
questions.answer: Sometimes they occupy a similar organizational role, but they usually encode dramatic tensions, permissions, relationships, and arcs rather than only combat abilities.

questions.question: Can two players use the same playbook?
questions.answer: The game decides. Many default to one of each because uniqueness supports niche and authority, while others allow duplicates.

questions.question: Can I optimize a PbtA character?
questions.answer: You can make informed choices, but most games reward engaging trouble and theme rather than avoiding every complication.

questions.question: Are high modifiers always best?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Repeated strong hits may reduce complications, while misses may grant experience or create desired drama. The game's incentives matter.

questions.question: Why are modifiers usually small?
questions.answer: Classic 2d6 bands are sensitive to each +1; large bonuses can nearly eliminate a result band.

questions.question: Can modifiers stack?
questions.answer: Only as the specific rules allow. Forward, ongoing, aid, conditions, and situational modifiers may have distinct limits.

questions.question: What is fictional positioning?
questions.answer: The established facts that determine whether an action is possible, which move applies, and what its outcome can accomplish.

questions.question: Can gear give bonuses?
questions.answer: Sometimes. Gear may instead grant permission, scale, range, protection, or tags without a numeric bonus.

questions.question: Can I roll to do the impossible?
questions.answer: No. Change the fiction first by gaining tools, access, scale, permission, or a different objective.

questions.question: Should the facilitator announce a move's name?
questions.answer: The game may encourage or discourage this. Clarity matters more than hiding procedure.

questions.question: What is a soft move?
questions.answer: A warning or developing consequence that leaves clear room to respond.

questions.question: What is a hard move?
questions.answer: A consequence applied decisively when the rules and established fiction authorize it.

questions.question: Can the facilitator make a hard move whenever desired?
questions.answer: No. Hardness should follow the game's triggers, agenda, principles, warnings, and established opportunities.

questions.question: What does play to find out mean?
questions.answer: Prepare active people, pressures, and situations without deciding the protagonists' choices or final outcome.

questions.question: Does play to find out mean no preparation?
questions.answer: No. Many games prescribe focused preparation such as threats, mysteries, countdowns, factions, questions, or locations.

questions.question: Can I use a prewritten adventure?
questions.answer: Yes, if adapted so it presents situations and pressures rather than requiring predetermined choices or outcomes.

questions.question: How do mysteries work?
questions.answer: They vary. Some have a prepared answer; others, such as Brindlewood Bay-style designs, use clues and a theory procedure.

questions.question: How do I set difficulty?
questions.answer: Many classic PbtA moves do not vary a target number. Difficulty appears through fictional positioning, costs, move selection, threats, limited effect, or game-specific modifiers.

questions.question: Can I add advantage and disadvantage?
questions.answer: Only if the game defines them or you intentionally design a tested house rule. Rolling three dice and keeping two changes probabilities substantially.

questions.question: Should every risky action trigger a move?
questions.answer: No. Only actions matching a rule's trigger use that rule.

questions.question: Can several moves trigger from one action?
questions.answer: Possibly. Use the game's instructions and resolve in an order that preserves fictional causality without double-charging the same consequence.

questions.question: Can one move cover a long montage?
questions.answer: Yes if its scope and trigger support it; otherwise use repeated scenes, a project, a clock, or a custom montage move.

questions.question: How long should a move's result last?
questions.answer: Use its text. If unclear, establish a concrete fictional duration or ending condition.

questions.question: Who chooses options on a move?
questions.answer: The move should say. Never assume the roller, facilitator, or target chooses.

questions.question: Must a facilitator answer move-granted questions truthfully?
questions.answer: Yes, within the move's wording and the game's honesty rules. A successful information move should not be secretly invalidated.

questions.question: Can the GM weaken a strong hit to protect a plot?
questions.answer: No. Honor the move's promise and let the prepared situation change.

questions.question: Can a player undo a consequence by explaining a better action after the roll?
questions.answer: Usually no; clarify intent and stakes before resolution. Use explicit resistance, flashback, or revision procedures if the game has them.

questions.question: What should happen after a roll?
questions.answer: Apply every choice and consequence, update the fiction and records, show who is affected, then continue the conversation.

questions.question: How do I make a custom move?
questions.answer: Start with a recurring fictional situation the game cares about, define its trigger and authority, choose an outcome structure, test every result, and revise from play.

questions.question: Should every custom move use 2d6?
questions.answer: No. Choose the resolution model that expresses the decision and uncertainty you want.

questions.question: Can I copy a move from another game?
questions.answer: Check copyright, permission, and license. Ideas and procedures require different legal treatment from exact protected wording.

questions.question: Can I call my game PbtA?
questions.answer: Under the creators' policy, the label is self-applied when Apocalypse World is a meaningful inspiration and the publishing policy is followed.

questions.question: Can I use the PbtA logo?
questions.answer: The official policy says to ask the creators for permission to use their logo.

questions.question: Are PbtA games mechanically compatible?
questions.answer: No. Similar vocabulary can hide different triggers, authority, probability, harm, and campaign assumptions.

questions.question: How do I convert a character from D&D?
questions.answer: Convert concept, relationships, signature permissions, and dramatic tensions; do not translate levels, armor class, spell slots, or exact numbers one-for-one.

questions.question: How do I choose a PbtA game?
questions.answer: Choose by premise, recurring activities, emotional intensity, facilitator model, campaign length, and the procedures you want to use repeatedly.

questions.question: What should players read first?
questions.answer: The premise, playbook, basic moves, relationship rules, harm or condition rules, advancement, and safety procedures.

questions.question: What should a facilitator read first?
questions.answer: The agenda, principles, GM moves, first-session procedure, preparation chapter, basic moves, harm, and campaign procedures.

questions.question: Can I run without reading the GM chapter?
questions.answer: That is risky. In PbtA games, facilitator instructions are often core rules rather than optional advice.

questions.question: How do I teach a first session?
questions.answer: Explain the conversation, have players describe actions, introduce moves only when triggered, and teach resources as they arise.

questions.question: How much lore should be created before play?
questions.answer: Only enough to support the premise and any facts the game requires. Leave questions open when the game expects discovery through play.

questions.question: What if two rules conflict?
questions.answer: Use the more specific current rule, then the game's stated priority or errata. Make a temporary transparent ruling if play must continue.

questions.question: What if a move's strict application feels wrong?
questions.answer: Pause before rolling or resolving, explain the mismatch, check the wording and purpose, and agree on an accommodation without secretly changing the result afterward.

questions.question: Can safety tools interrupt a move?
questions.answer: Yes. Real-world safety procedures always take priority over in-fiction continuity.

questions.question: Do lines and veils reduce dramatic play?
questions.answer: No. Clear boundaries help players commit confidently to the material that remains.

questions.question: Can a character die?
questions.answer: Only according to the chosen game's harm and end-state rules; some games make death common, rare, negotiated, or impossible.

questions.question: Can a campaign continue after a playbook is resolved?
questions.answer: Often yes through playbook change, retirement, replacement characters, legacy play, or a transformed role.

questions.question: What is the best PbtA game for beginners?
questions.answer: There is no universal answer. The best choice is the game whose premise excites the group and whose complexity and subject matter fit them.

questions.question: Is Blades in the Dark PbtA?
questions.answer: Its creator identification is recognized in the official PbtA directory, and it also founded the distinct Forged in the Dark family.

questions.question: Is Ironsworn PbtA?
questions.answer: It is a PbtA-inspired game with a distinct action-die versus challenge-dice system and solo/co-op/guided modes.

questions.question: Can I use this JSON instead of a rulebook?
questions.answer: No. It is a system-family teaching and implementation reference; the specific game's current rules always control.

legacy_reference_archive.note: The original v1 researched guide is preserved verbatim in data structure so no substantive section is lost. The expanded sections are the preferred indexes.

metadata.title: How to Play Powered by the Apocalypse
metadata.subtitle: A Current, System-Neutral Guide to the PbtA Family of Tabletop Roleplaying Games
intended_audience: players coming from D&D, Pathfinder, Call of Cthulhu, or other task-resolution RPGs
first-time PbtA GMs, MCs, Keepers, and facilitators
experienced groups comparing different PbtA implementations
software and rules-reference developers needing normalized structured data

scope.primary: The shared play procedures and design patterns commonly found across Powered by the Apocalypse games.
scope.secondary: The classic Apocalypse World-style 2d6 resolution model and common PbtA vocabulary.
not_in_scope: A replacement for the complete rules of any specific PbtA game.
A claim that every PbtA game uses 2d6, playbooks, moves, a GM, harm, or advancement.
Complete copyrighted move lists, playbook text, setting text, or proprietary examples.
A universal combat, magic, equipment, or character-creation subsystem, because no such universal subsystem exists.

metadata.copyright_and_use_note: This file is an original explanatory summary and teaching aid. It paraphrases common procedures, identifies publicly documented patterns, and links to official sources. Use the complete rules and play materials for the specific PbtA game being played.
metadata.archive_role: Version 1.0.0 baseline retained inside the expanded database.
metadata.superseded_by: Powered by the Apocalypse Complete Play Reference Database v2.0.0

edition_identity.direct_answer: Powered by the Apocalypse is not a single game system with one universal edition. It is a self-applied family label for games inspired by Apocalypse World or by other PbtA games.

latest_edition_interpretation_used_for_t.framework: Current official PbtA design and play guidance published by Meguey and Vincent Baker, including material through 2026.
latest_edition_interpretation_used_for_t.latest_apocalypse_world_development: A preview of Apocalypse World 3rd Edition core playbooks and rules was released to backers at the end of April 2026. Official May 2026 articles describe it as a preview and refer to a future final book.
latest_edition_interpretation_used_for_t.stable_complete_apocalypse_world_referen: Apocalypse World 2nd Edition, published in 2016, remains the most accessible complete official reference set used here for classic examples.
current_family_examples: Monster of the Week hardcover edition and its 2025-2026 official reference materials

rules_priority: Use the exact rules of the specific PbtA game and edition at your table.
Use that game's playbooks, basic-move sheets, GM materials, and errata.
Use this file to understand shared habits of play and to identify which questions must be answered by the chosen game.
When this file and a specific game's rules differ, the specific game always wins.
edition_identity.important_consequence: There is no safe universal character sheet, move list, combat sequence, damage track, spell system, initiative system, or advancement table for all PbtA games.

executive_summary.one_sentence: Describe what the characters do in the fiction; when a rule or move applies, follow it exactly; let the result change the situation; then continue the conversation and play to find out what happens.
core_loop: The GM or another player describes the current fictional situation.
A player says what their character does, wants, asks, or attempts.
The table determines whether a move or other rule applies.
If no rule applies, resolve the action through the established fiction and continue.
If a move applies, follow its procedure, including any roll, choices, questions, costs, or automatic effects.
Apply the result as a real change in the fiction.
The GM and players describe the consequences, shift the spotlight, and ask what happens next.
executive_summary.most_important_difference_from_many_trad: Players normally do not select a generic skill check whenever they attempt something uncertain. Rolls happen when the fiction and the game's rules bring a move into play.
executive_summary.best_beginner_rule: Do not begin with the dice. Begin by saying what the character actually does.

before_play.instruction: Choose one specific PbtA game whose premise matches the story the group wants.
before_play.why: PbtA games are tightly designed around particular genres, conflicts, and themes.

before_play.instruction: Read that game's premise, player principles, basic moves, playbooks, and GM agenda/principles.
before_play.why: The exact text determines what the game is about and how authority is shared.

before_play.instruction: Hold a session-zero conversation about tone, subject matter, safety tools, campaign length, and the kinds of conflict everyone wants.
before_play.why: Many PbtA games create emotionally charged, interpersonal, horrific, romantic, political, or violent situations.

before_play.instruction: Choose playbooks or other character frameworks, then follow the game's creation steps in order.
before_play.why: Character creation often creates the setting, relationships, and opening situation at the same time.

before_play.instruction: Answer relationship and setting questions aloud, recording only what the game asks you to record.
before_play.why: The group's answers are usable fiction, not decorative backstory.

during_play.instruction: The facilitator frames an immediate situation and asks a character what they do.
The player answers in fictional terms, not only with a move name.
When a move applies, resolve it and make every listed choice or consequence matter.
On a mixed result or miss, change the situation instead of stalling or merely saying 'nothing happens.'
End scenes and sessions using the game's own recovery, experience, relationship, and end-of-session procedures.

minimum_materials: The chosen game's rulebook or quickstart
Its current basic-move and GM reference sheets
One character playbook or sheet per player, when the game uses them
The dice, cards, tokens, or other randomizer specified by that game
A way to record conditions, harm, resources, relationships, clocks, or experience

is: A family of games connected by inspiration and self-identification.
An approach in which procedures shape a focused conversation about a particular kind of fiction.
A tradition of designing rules, moves, playbooks, GM instructions, and advancement around the game's themes.
A style that often distributes narrative authority through explicit questions, options, and procedures.
A family in which consequences normally create forward motion.
is_not: A universal open rules engine with one canonical rulebook.
Required to use playbooks, moves, stats, or a traditional GM.
A guarantee that two PbtA games are mechanically compatible.
An instruction to improvise without rules or preparation.
A license to ignore the exact wording of the chosen game's procedures.
what_pbta_is_and_is_not.self_identification_rule: A game's creator is the relevant authority on whether the game is PbtA, because the label describes its inspiration.

core_play_principles.name: The conversation is the base system
core_play_principles.explanation: Play is an exchange of descriptions, questions, decisions, reactions, and procedures. Character sheets and dice enter the conversation when called upon, then hand play back to the fiction.

core_play_principles.name: Fiction and mechanics continually affect each other
core_play_principles.explanation: Fictional facts determine whether an action is possible, dangerous, costly, or move-triggering. Mechanical results create new fictional facts that must be honored.

core_play_principles.name: Play to find out
core_play_principles.explanation: Prepare pressures, people, threats, places, and motives, but do not decide the protagonists' choices or the final outcome in advance.

core_play_principles.name: Use specific procedures instead of defaulting to generic checks
core_play_principles.explanation: A roll is justified by the chosen game's move or procedure, not merely by uncertainty.

core_play_principles.name: Every result changes the situation
core_play_principles.explanation: A strong hit, mixed result, miss, automatic effect, spent resource, or chosen option should become visible in what happens next.

core_play_principles.name: Honor the move's exact promises
core_play_principles.explanation: When a move grants questions, choices, protection, harm, information, or authority, provide it. Do not secretly weaken a success because the GM preferred another outcome.

core_play_principles.name: Fictional positioning matters before and after the roll
core_play_principles.explanation: The character's approach, tools, leverage, location, relationships, and opposition can determine whether a move can happen and what its result can accomplish.

core_play_principles.name: Share the spotlight
core_play_principles.explanation: Move between characters at moments of tension, invite quieter players, and avoid letting one player make every decision or roll.

core_play_principles.name: Questions and answers are often mechanical procedures
core_play_principles.explanation: When the rules require an honest answer or a specific question, that exchange is part of resolution, not optional flavor.

core_play_principles.name: Genre is built into the rules
core_play_principles.explanation: A PbtA game's moves identify the actions, dilemmas, relationships, and consequences that the game wants to revisit.

core_play_principles.name: Rules are a shared agreement with humane flexibility
core_play_principles.explanation: Current Apocalypse World 3rd Edition preview commentary describes moves as frameworks with designed tolerance. The group may discuss a move when its strict application does not land, but should preserve the game's underlying purpose and return to the written rule as the stable baseline.

responsibilities: Portray a protagonist honestly and actively.
Say what the character does in the fiction.
Follow mandatory move triggers and procedures.
Make choices granted by moves.
Answer questions truthfully when the rules require it.
Track the resources assigned to the player.
Respect the established fiction and other players' authority over their own characters.
Pursue the playbook's pressures, relationships, drives, or themes rather than trying to avoid every complication.
not_responsible_for: Protecting the character from all trouble.
Winning through optimal action-economy play unless the specific game explicitly centers that.

responsibilities: Follow the chosen game's agenda, principles, rules, and GM moves.
Describe the world and portray non-player characters.
Ask questions and use the answers.
Present pressures and consequences without predetermining the protagonists' choices.
Apply the results of player moves honestly.
Make GM moves when the game instructs or the conversation demands a response.
Keep events moving and distribute spotlight.
Prepare only the kinds of material the game requests.
not_responsible_for: Writing a fixed plot that the players must follow.
Rolling to oppose every player action unless the game explicitly says so.
Hiding all relevant stakes until after a choice.
Neutral refereeing divorced from the game's agenda and principles.

gm_less_and_coop_variants.note: Some PbtA games are GMless, co-GMed, solo, or use rotating authority.
procedure: Identify who answers each category of question.
Use oracles, prompts, cards, structured scenes, or shared roles exactly as the game directs.
Do not import a traditional GM by default when the game intentionally distributes that authority.

goals: Confirm the exact game and edition or playtest version.
Explain the premise in one or two sentences.
Agree on campaign or one-shot length.
Discuss tone, intensity, humor, romance, horror, violence, and intra-party conflict.
Choose safety tools and establish how anyone can pause, revise, or remove content.
Explain whether player-versus-player moves are possible and how consent will be handled.
Explain what information players control about their own characters.
Review the basic moves and the GM agenda.
Create characters together so relationship questions can be answered in context.
Record unresolved questions as material to discover during play, not as errors to eliminate.

recommended_categories: veils: content that may exist but is not described in detail
aftercare and debrief for intense sessions
check-ins when a move would control, alter, expose, or pressure another player character
safety_baseline.important_note: Safety procedures supplement the game's rules and can always interrupt them.

expectation_reset_for_traditional_rpg_pl: You may roll less often, but each roll can have broader consequences.
A 7-9 is usually a hit with a cost, complication, reduced effect, or hard choice, not simply a failed roll.
A miss gives the game permission to change the situation; it does not always mean the character looked incompetent.
The GM may not roll dice at all.
Combat may use the same conversation and move structure as every other scene.
Your playbook is a dramatic role and pressure structure, not only a combat class.

character_creation.universal_warning: There is no universal PbtA character-creation method. Use the ordered steps on the chosen game's playbook or sheet.

common_components.purpose: Focuses the character's dramatic role, resources, special moves, and likely conflicts.
Creates an immediately playable person rather than a stat block.
Modify moves or represent changing self-concepts, competencies, emotions, or methods.
Give the character distinctive permissions, procedures, and ways to affect the conversation.
Mechanically connect protagonists and create immediate reasons to interact.
Establish fictional permissions, tags, scarcity, and signature capabilities.
Create setting details, vulnerabilities, goals, and material the GM should bring into play.
Define how danger, pressure, sacrifice, or limited protection works in that game.

best_practices: Create characters in the same room or call whenever possible.
Read the playbook introduction and all chosen moves.
Do not assume two playbooks with similar powers tell the same kind of story.
Treat every relationship answer as permission to create scenes around it.
Leave blanks that the rules intend the group to discover later.
Avoid writing a private novel-length backstory that conflicts with group creation.

choose_by: the kind of pressure you want the character to face
the relationships you want to explore
the decisions you want to make repeatedly
the genre role you want to embody
do_not_choose_only_by: a superficial resemblance to a class in another RPG

questions: Where is everyone?
What is happening right now?
What is immediately obvious?
What has already been established as true?

cycle.procedure: The GM or current speaker asks what a character does, or a player takes initiative by describing an action.

questions: What are you trying to accomplish?
How are you doing it?
What tools, leverage, or position are you relying on?
What danger or resistance is present?

cycle.procedure: Determine whether a move, resource rule, harm rule, relationship rule, or other procedure applies.
Follow the procedure completely, including choices and questions.
Describe how the mechanical result appears in the fiction.
Shift the situation, spotlight, or stakes and ask what happens next.

possible_outcomes: The action simply happens because the fiction permits it.
The GM explains why it cannot happen under the established circumstances.
The GM states the possible consequence or required fictional step and asks what the player does.
Another character or threat reacts according to the fiction.
The table asks for more detail until it is clear whether a move applies.
when_no_move_triggers.do_not: Invent a generic 2d6 roll merely because the outcome feels uncertain, unless the chosen game gives a catch-all move or explicit rule for doing so.

moves.definition: A move is a rule that organizes part of the conversation. It may be triggered by fiction, chosen directly, invoked by procedure, or operate without a fictional trigger.

common_anatomy.trigger_or_timing: When, whether, or how the move enters play.
common_anatomy.fictional_requirements: What must be true, what the character must actually do, and what target or situation must exist.
common_anatomy.mechanical_instruction: Roll, choose, spend, ask, hold, mark, compare, draw, or apply an automatic effect.
common_anatomy.result_branches: What happens on each result band or choice.
common_anatomy.authority: Who chooses, answers, or describes each part.
common_anatomy.follow_through: How the result changes ongoing fiction.

trigger_patterns.description: The move becomes mandatory when its described event happens in the fiction.
trigger_patterns.table_habit: Anyone may point out that the trigger has occurred; pause and resolve it.

trigger_patterns.description: The player can intentionally have the character take the action named by the move.
trigger_patterns.table_habit: Clarify what the character does, confirm fictional permission, then use the move.

trigger_patterns.description: The move occurs at session start, session end, when harm is suffered, when a resource changes, or at another rules-defined time.
The player may invoke the move without first satisfying a fictional trigger, when the move says so.
An instruction for how the GM changes or responds to the fiction; normally narrated as events rather than announced by rule name.

traditional_to_do_it_do_it_guidance.meaning: When a move has a fictional trigger, the character must actually do the triggering thing in the fiction; conversely, when the character does it, the group should not skip the move.
does_not_mean: The player must quote the move's title.
The player can press a move like a video-game button without describing an approach.
The GM may deny a clearly triggered move merely to preserve a planned outcome.

disagreement_procedure.current_apocalypse_world_3e_preview_infl: Official 2026 preview commentary instructs participants who disagree about a move to explain themselves and pause until they work it out.
system_neutral_steps: Pause the fiction before adding new consequences.
Each person explains what they believe the move requires or promises.
Check the move text, surrounding rules, agenda, and principles.
Clarify the fictional facts and each person's intended outcome.
Agree on the written interpretation, a mutually acceptable exception, or a return to the strict written baseline.
Use a safety tool or stop the scene if the disagreement concerns boundaries or player agency.

result_integrity: Do not make a player roll again to receive the success already granted.
Do not convert every strong hit into a hidden complication.
Do not treat every miss as the literal opposite of the attempted action.
Do not omit choices or questions because the GM thinks the answer is obvious.
Do not let an option exceed what the established fiction can coherently support without discussing it.

classic_2d6_resolution.status: Common and historically important, but not universal to PbtA.
classic_2d6_resolution.formula: Roll 2d6 and add the stat or modifier named by the move.

typical_result_bands.label: strong hit
typical_result_bands.generic_meaning: The move's strongest listed result applies, often with greater effect, more choices, or fewer costs.

typical_result_bands.label: weak hit or mixed result
typical_result_bands.generic_meaning: The move succeeds according to its text, but with reduced effect, a cost, exposure, a complication, a choice, or shared authority.

typical_result_bands.label: miss
typical_result_bands.generic_meaning: Follow the move's miss text. When it has no explicit miss clause, the GM commonly makes an appropriate move according to the game's rules.

typical_result_bands.label: advanced or exceptional result in some games
typical_result_bands.generic_meaning: Only applies when the chosen game or an advanced move explicitly defines it.

critical_rolls.natural_12: Usually has no special meaning by itself unless the game says it does.
critical_rolls.snake_eyes: Usually has no special meaning by itself unless the game says it does.
critical_rolls.rule: Read the final modified total and the move's text.

probability_table.assumptions: Unmodified 2d6 distribution; no rerolls, advantage systems, bonuses after the roll, or move-specific alterations.
interpretation: At +0, a strong hit occurs 16.67% of the time, a 7-9 occurs 41.67%, and a miss occurs 41.67%.
At +1, the most common band is 7-9 at 44.44%.
At +3, strong hits become more likely than the other bands, but misses still occur 8.33% of the time.
Small modifiers are powerful because they shift results across two thresholds.

advanced_12_plus_probability.warning: A 12+ result is not universal and often requires an advanced move.

rolling_procedure: Confirm the move and its named modifier.
Clarify any relevant fictional facts before rolling.
Apply only bonuses and penalties authorized by the game.
Make every required choice and answer every required question.
Describe and apply the result before making another roll.

mixed_results.not_a_generic_rule: There is no universal menu of partial-success complications.
mixed_results.correct_method: Use the exact 7-9 text of the move.
common_forms: the GM chooses part of the result
the player chooses an unwanted consequence

not_always_failure: The character may accomplish the immediate task but expose themselves to a worse problem.
The GM may reveal unwelcome information.
A resource may be lost or depleted.
The action may separate characters or put someone in a spot.
The move's own miss clause may grant a limited effect.
Another authority may describe what goes wrong.
misses.best_test: Choose a consequence that follows from the established fiction, honors the game's agenda and principles, and creates a meaningful next decision.

non_2d6_variants.core_fact: PbtA games may use other dice, dice pools, cards, tokens, diceless procedures, scene structures, or no randomizer.

documented_examples.variation: Uses an Apocalypse World-like three-band roll but assigns modifiers to individual 'plays' rather than character stats.
Uses cards and cumulative card values rather than the classic 2d6 roll.

non_2d6_variants.adaptation_rule: Do not translate a non-2d6 PbtA game back into 2d6 unless deliberately designing a hack. Follow its native procedure.

fictional_positioning.definition: The established circumstances that determine what actions are possible, what rules apply, and what an outcome can reasonably accomplish.

dimensions.question: Can the character do this at all with their current abilities, access, and tools?
Does this approach satisfy the move's conditions?
What can this action meaningfully change?
What can the opposition or environment do in response?
Is the character acting against one person, a gang, an institution, a storm, or an army?
What reason, evidence, relationship, threat, promise, or vulnerability makes the action effective?
What do range, area, messy, armor, magical, intimate, loud, or other game-specific tags establish?

examples.situation: A locked office door with ordinary tools and no immediate pressure.
examples.likely_handling: The character may simply open it after enough time, or the GM may ask how they obtain the needed tools; no move is automatically required.

examples.situation: The same lock while guards approach and alarms are active.
examples.likely_handling: A danger- or pressure-related move may trigger because the risk is now part of the action.

examples.situation: A character shoots an unaware, helpless target at point-blank range.
examples.likely_handling: Some games apply harm as established rather than using a symmetric combat roll.

examples.situation: A character tries to command a ruler with no status, leverage, threat, or supernatural power.
examples.likely_handling: A manipulation move may not trigger; the fiction may require leverage first.

forward.typical_meaning: A bonus or penalty to the next qualifying roll, then it is consumed.
forward.warning: Exact duration and qualification are game-specific.

ongoing.typical_meaning: A bonus or penalty that applies repeatedly while a stated condition remains true.
ongoing.warning: Do not assume it applies to every roll.

hold.typical_meaning: A temporary currency generated by a move and spent on that move's listed effects.
hold.rule: Unspent hold lasts only as long as the move says.

take_plus_one.typical_meaning: Add one to the specified roll or category of rolls.

mark.typical_meaning: Record a box, condition, experience, harm, resource, or other change.

as_established.typical_meaning: Use the harm, position, scale, tags, and consequences already made true in the fiction and rules.

choice_menu.typical_meaning: Select exactly the number of options granted; unchosen options are not automatically true.

ask_questions.typical_meaning: Spend the granted questions or hold and receive the honest information promised by the move.

conditions.typical_meaning: Named emotional, physical, social, or narrative states that affect play and have specific clearing procedures.

tags.typical_meaning: Compact descriptors that create fictional and sometimes numerical effects.

clock_or_countdown.typical_meaning: A structured display of worsening threat, progress, scarcity, or approaching events.

strings_bonds_hx_influence_debts.typical_meaning: Different games' relationship currencies or ratings.

combat_and_danger.universal_warning: There is no universal PbtA combat system.
common_characteristics: Combat usually remains part of the same conversation used for every other scene.
Many games have no separate initiative roll or fixed turn order.
The GM may not roll attacks for NPCs.
One move can represent a moment, exchange, chase segment, tactical objective, or whole skirmish depending on the game and fiction.
Harm may be exchanged automatically when a move says so.
Position, range, cover, weapons, armor, numbers, and intent matter through fiction and tags.
Enemies may be represented by moves, harm capacity, conditions, clocks, qualities, or narrative permissions rather than full player-style stat blocks.
combat_procedure: Establish positions, goals, immediate threats, and what is at stake.
Ask a player what their character does.
Identify the move or rule, if any, that matches the action and situation.
Resolve it once; do not divide one coherent action into unnecessary sub-rolls.
Apply harm, conditions, costs, separation, lost position, or other effects as written.
Describe the enemy and environment's response through GM moves or the result text.
Shift spotlight before one character monopolizes the whole fight.
End the fight when the fiction says the objective is achieved, abandoned, or impossible.

initiative.default_assumption: No universal initiative or action economy.
spotlight_method: Give threatened characters a chance to respond when appropriate.
Return to players who have not acted recently.
Use the game's specific battle procedures when they override free spotlight management.

enemy_actions.common_method: The GM describes an incoming threat, consequence, or completed action according to the game's GM-move rules.

distinguish.soft_move: Signals danger, offers an opportunity, or presents a consequence that the players can still address.
distinguish.hard_move: Makes an immediate, concrete, difficult-to-reverse consequence happen.

enemy_actions.warning: Soft and hard are descriptive concepts, not universal formal labels in every game.

avoid: Calling for repeated attack rolls until hit points reach zero unless the game is designed that way.
Giving NPCs a hidden traditional action economy.
Ignoring a strong hit because an enemy was intended to survive.
Assuming combat is the only place where moves can have severe consequences.
Using harm as the only meaningful stake.

harm_conditions_and_recovery.universal_warning: Every chosen game defines its own danger and recovery model.
possible_models: retirement, transformation, or loss of control
how_to_apply: Use the amount or condition established by the move, weapon, threat, or fiction.
Apply armor or reduction only where the game allows.
Describe the concrete effect, not only the marked box.
Use any required harm move, condition move, or instability procedure.
Follow the exact recovery trigger and do not import rests from another RPG.

monster_of_the_week_example_as_variation.purpose: Demonstrates how one current PbtA game combines a harm track, armor, instability, Luck, and experience.
summary: Armor reduces harm by its rating.
Serious wounds can become unstable and worsen without treatment.
Luck can alter a roll or negate a wound, but is limited.
Experience can be marked on misses and through end-of-session questions.

death_and_character_loss.rule: Read the chosen game's procedure before the first dangerous scene.
session_zero_questions: Does a player choose death, retirement, or transformation?
What happens to the player after a character leaves play?

relationships_and_player_vs_player.importance: Many PbtA games place relationships at the center of resolution and advancement.
pvp_guidance: Use the exact player-versus-player procedure, because many moves distinguish PCs from NPCs.
Do not let a social move erase another player's authority over their character unless the rule explicitly and consensually permits that effect.
State desired outcomes before rolling when the move asks for them.
Use safety tools for coercion, intimacy, betrayal, mind control, or identity-changing effects.
When a move grants another player a choice, preserve that choice.

advancement.universal_warning: There is no universal level system.
common_xp_triggers: fulfilling drives, keys, beliefs, playbook prompts, or relationship triggers
common_improvements: increase a stat within a cap
gain a move from another playbook
gain gear, resources, followers, territory, or a team feature
create or play an additional character
transform the campaign or character's role
best_practices: Review every XP trigger before play.
Mark experience immediately when the trigger occurs.
Choose improvements that create new fictional possibilities, not only larger numbers.
Discuss major playbook changes or retirement with the group.

core_structure.agenda: The broad outcomes and priorities the GM must pursue.
core_structure.principles: The decision-making rules that shape every description, judgment, and move.
core_structure.always_say_or_rules: Constraints on what the GM may state and what sources of truth must be honored.
core_structure.gm_moves: Concrete ways to change the fiction when the GM has the opportunity or obligation.
core_structure.prep_procedure: The game's approved method for creating threats, fronts, mysteries, arcs, factions, clocks, or situations.

classic_apocalypse_world_style_agenda_su: Make the fictional world feel real.
Make the protagonists' lives active and consequential rather than dull.
Play to find out what happens.
common_principle_patterns: Ask provocative questions and build on the answers.
Be a fan of the protagonists while making their lives difficult.
Give non-player characters names, motives, humanity, and concrete behavior.
Think about events outside the current scene.
Use consequences that follow from the fiction.
Do not speak the name of a GM move as though announcing an ability.

common_apocalypse_world_style_opportunit: A player rolls a miss and the move does not fully specify the result.
Everyone looks to the GM to learn what happens.
The players hand the GM a clear fictional opportunity.
A rule, countdown, threat, or move explicitly instructs the GM to act.
when_to_make_a_gm_move.warning: Use the chosen game's list and timing rules; some games structure facilitator actions differently.

generic_gm_move_families: reveal danger or future trouble
show off-screen consequences
separate characters
put someone in a difficult position
inflict established harm or another established cost
take away or threaten a resource
offer an opportunity with or without a cost
turn a move's consequences back toward the characters
advance a threat or countdown
present a difficult choice
tell the possible consequences and ask whether the character proceeds
shift attention to another character or location
gm_move_selection_test: Does it follow from what has already been established?
Does it respect the result the player earned?
Does it create a concrete next decision?
Is its severity appropriate to the setup and timing?
Will the players understand what changed?

soft.function: Telegraph, threaten, reveal, position, or offer a chance to respond.
examples: The bridge cables begin snapping one by one.
The detective reaches for the evidence bag.
You hear the monster in the room behind you.

hard.function: Apply an immediate and concrete consequence.
examples: The bridge gives way beneath you.
The detective takes the evidence and orders your arrest.
The monster crashes through the wall and separates you from the others.

soft_and_hard_moves.severity_rule: A hard move should normally be supported by prior setup, a miss, an ignored danger, a golden opportunity, or a rule that authorizes it.

prepare: threats and what they will do if unopposed
questions you genuinely want play to answer
countdowns, fronts, mysteries, factions, or arcs required by the game
do_not_prepare: a sequence of scenes that must occur in order
a final outcome that invalidates move results
prep.clue_guidance: Do not make essential forward progress depend on repeatedly guessing the correct question or succeeding on one hidden check. Use the game's investigation moves and threat structure to deliver actionable information and new decisions.

player_best_practices.example: Instead of saying only 'I use the manipulation move,' explain what you want and what leverage, promise, pressure, or appeal you use.
Choose actions that expose the character's conflicts and relationships rather than avoiding every trigger.
Ask what the character can see, what is dangerous, what a move requires, and what the stakes are before rolling.
A cost changes what you face; it does not require surrendering control over your character beyond what the rule grants.
Spend hold, Luck, Strings, Team, or similar resources when their fictional moment matters.
Answer the GM's questions with concrete, usable details and leave room for other players.
After a major choice or reveal, invite another character's reaction.

gm_preparation: Know the premise, agenda, principles, basic moves, and each selected playbook.
Prepare names, impressions, possible threats, and open questions rather than a plot.
Know the opening situation or follow the game's procedure for creating it.
recommended_flow: Introduce the premise and safety tools.
Summarize the relationships and immediate setting aloud.
Begin in a situation that demands a choice now.
Ask direct questions and build on answers.
Use early moves to teach the resolution bands.
Give every character a meaningful interaction.
End with the game's session-end procedure.
first_session_gm_priorities: Learn what each character cares about.
Create links between characters and threats.
Find where the group lacks control.
Avoid explaining the entire campaign before play reveals it.

setup: Use a game or quickstart designed for one-shots when available.
Preselect or limit playbooks without removing meaningful choice.
Begin after the characters are already connected.
Use one urgent situation with a visible countdown or consequence.
Use faster advancement only if the game recommends it.
pacing: First quarter: establish characters, relationships, and immediate problem.
Second quarter: reveal the deeper pressure and force tradeoffs.
Third quarter: escalate consequences and expose character conflicts.
Final quarter: resolve the central question and perform end-of-session reflection.
avoid: A long tavern-style introduction with no pressure.
Multiple unrelated threats.
Saving every important revelation for the final minutes.
Treating misses as delays.

campaign_engine: Record the consequences of player choices.
Update threats, relationships, clocks, fronts, or mysteries between sessions.
Bring unresolved costs and promises back into play.
Let advancement change the kinds of stories the characters can create.
Ask whether the original premise is still the game everyone wants.
continuity: What promise, debt, injury, condition, or resource remains unresolved?
What are we now playing to find out?
endings: Use retirement, final advancements, endgame moves, or arc procedures when provided.
Let campaigns end when their central question has been answered.
Do not force indefinite play merely because characters can still improve.

five_minute_player_explanation: Say what your character does in the story.
You roll only when a move or rule applies.
In classic 2d6 games, 10+ is a strong result, 7-9 is a hit with limits or consequences, and 6- lets the game respond strongly.
Read the move every time until it becomes familiar.
Your choices and relationships matter more than optimizing a turn sequence.
five_minute_gm_explanation: Ask questions, use the answers, and present concrete situations.
On a GM move, change the fiction and create another decision.
Honor every success and every choice granted by the rules.
teaching_during_play: Before the first roll, identify the trigger aloud.
After the roll, read the relevant result aloud.
Ask the player to choose before describing the final outcome.
Translate the result into concrete fiction.
Explain one rule at the moment it becomes relevant rather than front-loading every subsystem.

worked_examples.label: No move is needed
worked_examples.fiction: The character has the office key, no one is watching, and nothing is pressuring them.
worked_examples.player_statement: I unlock the office and go inside.
worked_examples.resolution: The door opens. The GM describes what is inside. No roll is created merely because entering could lead to future trouble.
worked_examples.lesson: Moves resolve the situations they are designed for; they are not universal permission checks.

worked_examples.label: Original illustrative danger move
worked_examples.copyright_status: Original example written for this guide; not a published move.

sample_move.trigger: When you cross unstable ground while immediate danger closes in, roll +Nerve.
sample_move.10_plus: You get across and choose one advantage: keep your gear secure, bring someone with you, or reach a superior position.
sample_move.7_to_9: You get across, but choose one: leave something behind, arrive exposed, or allow the danger to advance.
sample_move.miss: The GM makes an appropriate move based on the collapsing route and approaching threat.

worked_examples.fiction: A character runs across a failing catwalk while security drones close in.
worked_examples.result: The player gets across and chooses to leave a heavy equipment case behind.
worked_examples.follow_through: The GM describes the case crashing into the machinery below and asks the next character whether they jump now or grab the case.
worked_examples.lesson: A 7-9 advances the character's goal and the danger at the same time.

worked_examples.label: A miss need not mean incompetence
worked_examples.fiction: A highly trained hunter examines a perfect crime scene while the culprit monitors the building.
worked_examples.poor_interpretation: The expert suddenly cannot recognize obvious evidence.
worked_examples.better_interpretation: The expert finds the evidence, but the culprit realizes exactly what they found and cuts power to the building.
worked_examples.lesson: Consequences can arise from opposition and changing circumstances rather than personal failure.

worked_examples.label: Fictional leverage before a social move
worked_examples.fiction: A character demands that a hostile official release a prisoner but offers no reason, threat, evidence, authority, or bargain.
worked_examples.resolution: The GM explains that the official has no reason to comply and asks what leverage the character creates.
worked_examples.next_action: The character reveals proof that the official's superior ordered the release.
worked_examples.move_check: Now the chosen game's manipulation or persuasion procedure may apply.
worked_examples.lesson: A high social stat does not automatically replace the fictional requirements of a move.

worked_examples.label: Combat is about fictional objectives
worked_examples.fiction: A character fires across a warehouse to stop a guard from reaching an alarm.
worked_examples.clarification: The goal is not simply to reduce the guard's hit points; it is to control movement before the alarm is triggered.
worked_examples.resolution: Use the move that matches suppressing, attacking, protecting, or acting under pressure in the chosen game.
worked_examples.follow_through: Apply the move's exact harm, position, or choice result and decide whether the alarm remains reachable.
worked_examples.lesson: The move follows intent, method, and situation, not a universal attack action.

worked_examples.label: Honor a strong hit
worked_examples.fiction: A move promises that on 10+ the character escapes cleanly.
worked_examples.incorrect_gm_response: You escape, but the enemy secretly tagged your vehicle and stole your supplies.
worked_examples.correct_gm_response: The character escapes cleanly. The GM advances unrelated off-screen events only if another rule authorizes it and it does not undermine the promised result.
worked_examples.lesson: Do not smuggle a mixed-result cost into a strong hit.

worked_examples.label: Pause when a move does not land
