worked_examples.fiction: A player chooses an option that another participant cannot reconcile with the established scale of the scene.
procedure: Pause.
Restate the move's promise.
Explain the fictional conflict.
Brainstorm an interpretation or mutually accepted adjustment.
Return to the written option if no adjustment is agreed.
Resume only after everyone understands what is now true.
worked_examples.lesson: The move text is the baseline of the table's agreement, not a weapon for overruling communication.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Treating PbtA as one universal 2d6 system
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Identify the exact game and use its native rules.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Rolling whenever an action is uncertain
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Ask whether a move or specific procedure applies. If not, resolve through fiction.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Calling a move by name without describing the action
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Clarify what the character actually does and wants.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Treating 7-9 as failure
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Apply the move's hit, then its cost, reduced effect, choice, or complication.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Making a miss mean 'nothing happens'
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Advance a threat, reveal something, inflict an established cost, or use the move's miss text.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Making every miss humiliating
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Let opposition, scarcity, timing, collateral danger, or external events create the consequence.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Using the same generic complication for every 7-9
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Read and apply the exact move.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Ignoring fictional position because the modifier is high
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Determine permission, trigger, scope, and effect before rolling.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Adding tactical turns and NPC attack rolls by habit
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Use spotlight and GM moves unless the game specifies a battle sequence.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Prewriting a plot
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Prepare threats, motives, places, and consequences, then play to find out.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Hiding all danger until after the roll
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Telegraph risks when the characters could reasonably perceive them.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Weakening a strong hit to preserve challenge
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Honor the result and make the next problem emerge honestly from the changed fiction.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Announcing GM move names
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Describe what happens in the world.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Assuming playbooks must be balanced like combat classes
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Evaluate spotlight, thematic authority, and narrative pressure, not only damage output.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Letting one character trigger every scene
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Cut the spotlight and ask other characters what they do.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Ignoring end-of-session procedures
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Reserve time for experience, relationship changes, recovery, and reflection.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Using 'fiction first' as permission to ignore rules
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Let fiction trigger rules and let rules change fiction; neither side erases the other.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Assuming the GM may control a player character's feelings or decisions
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Follow the exact authority granted by the move and use consent and disagreement procedures.

differences_between_pbta_games.compatibility_rule: A move, playbook, or subsystem from one PbtA game is not automatically balanced, meaningful, or mechanically compatible with another.

representative_games.title: Apocalypse World
representative_games.role_in_family: The original game that inspired the PbtA family.
representative_games.current_status_in_research: 2nd Edition is the stable complete reference; 3rd Edition core rules/playbooks were previewed in April 2026 and remain in development toward a final book.
representative_games.use_for_learning: Classic conversation, moves, playbooks, MC agenda/principles, threats, harm, and 2d6 bands.

representative_games.title: Monster of the Week
representative_games.current_status_in_research: Hardcover edition introduced in 2023, with current official downloadable play and reference materials dated 2025-2026.
representative_games.use_for_learning: Focused basic moves, mysteries, Keeper moves, threat countdowns, harm, Luck, and miss-based experience.

representative_games.title: Avatar Legends: The Roleplaying Game
representative_games.use_for_learning: Basic moves shared by all characters, playbook identity, balance, conditions, and genre-specific conflict.

representative_games.title: Masks: A New Generation
representative_games.role_in_family: A young-superhero PbtA game focused on identity and influence.
representative_games.use_for_learning: Labels, conditions, influence, emotional stakes, and playbooks as identity conflicts.

representative_games.title: Under Hollow Hills
representative_games.role_in_family: A PbtA game by the original creators that demonstrates major structural variation.
representative_games.use_for_learning: Moves called plays, move-specific modifiers, and voluntarily chosen moves.

representative_games.title: Murderous Ghosts
representative_games.role_in_family: An early PbtA game by the original creators that does not use classic dice resolution.
representative_games.use_for_learning: Card-based, tightly structured play and proof that 2d6 is not essential to the label.

player_before_a_move: Is the target or situation present?
Do I have the fictional permission, tools, position, or leverage?
Which exact move or rule applies?
player_after_a_move: Describe your character's part of the result.
gm_before_a_response: Has a move granted or restricted my authority?
What do my agenda and principles require?
Is this a soft setup or an authorized hard consequence?
What concrete choice will this create?
gm_between_sessions: Update threats, clocks, mysteries, fronts, or factions.
Record changes caused by the protagonists.
Review character flags, conditions, relationships, and advancement.
Do not write the protagonists' solution.
session_end: Ask what threads players want to continue.
Check in about tone, boundaries, and the session experience.

faq.question: What is the latest edition of Powered by the Apocalypse?
faq.answer: There is no universal edition. PbtA is a family label. Choose a specific PbtA game and use its latest rules. This guide uses current PbtA commentary through 2026, notes the Apocalypse World 3rd Edition preview, and uses Apocalypse World 2nd Edition as a complete classic reference.

faq.question: Do all PbtA games use 2d6 plus a stat?
faq.answer: No. The original Apocalypse World does, and many descendants do, but official PbtA examples also use other dice, cards, or no dice.

faq.question: Do players roll for everything difficult?
faq.answer: No. They roll or use another procedure when the game's rules call for it.

faq.question: Is 7-9 a failure?
faq.answer: Usually it is a hit with the exact limitations described by the move. Never replace the move's text with a universal partial-success rule.

faq.question: Does 6 or less always mean the attempted action fails?
faq.answer: No. Use the move's miss clause or the game's GM-move procedure. The action may succeed while the situation worsens.

faq.question: Can the GM change a move result?
faq.answer: The GM should apply the result honestly. The table may discuss a result that does not coherently land, but no participant should unilaterally erase another participant's granted choice or success.

faq.question: Who rolls for NPCs?
faq.answer: In many PbtA games the GM does not roll and NPC actions appear through GM moves and established consequences. Some games differ.

faq.question: Is there initiative?
faq.answer: Not universally. Many games use conversational spotlight. Some have special battle or exchange procedures.

faq.question: Can I mix playbooks and moves from different PbtA games?
faq.answer: Only as deliberate game design. Shared vocabulary does not ensure compatibility.

faq.question: What does 'fiction first' mean?
faq.answer: Begin with what is happening and what the character does, then use the rules that apply. It does not mean rules are optional.

faq.question: Can players say a move name?
faq.answer: Yes, but the group still needs to understand the fictional action and trigger when the move has one.

faq.question: How much should the GM prepare?
faq.answer: Prepare the threats, people, places, motives, questions, and structures requested by the game; do not predetermine the characters' decisions or ending.

faq.question: Are playbooks classes?
faq.answer: They can organize abilities like classes, but they also define dramatic pressures, relationships, resources, and thematic questions.

faq.question: How do I know how hard a GM move should be?
faq.answer: Use the fictional setup, the trigger that gave the GM an opportunity, the game's agenda and principles, and prior warnings. Make consequences understandable and proportionate.

faq.question: What should I read first for a new PbtA game?
faq.answer: Read the premise, basic moves, selected playbooks, player principles, GM agenda/principles/moves, harm or condition rules, and first-session procedure.

glossary.definition: Powered by the Apocalypse; a self-applied family label for games inspired by Apocalypse World or other PbtA games.
A rule that structures a particular part of the conversation.
A move generally available to every player character in games that use this structure.
A character framework combining identity, moves, resources, relationships, advancement, and thematic pressure.
A facilitator instruction for changing or responding to the fiction.
The facilitator's mandatory high-level goals.
A rule for how the facilitator makes decisions and portrays the game.
The condition, event, choice, or timing that brings a move into play.
The high result band, commonly 10+ in classic 2d6 games.
The middle result band, commonly 7-9 in classic 2d6 games.
The low result band or failed procedure, commonly 6 or less in classic 2d6 games; its meaning is defined by the move and GM rules.
The imagined people, places, events, capabilities, positions, and facts established in play.
The circumstances that determine permission, risk, trigger, scope, and effect.
A temporary move-generated resource spent on listed options.
A modifier applied to the next qualifying roll, in many games.
A modifier that continues while its stated condition remains true, in many games.
Apply the harm already justified by weapons, armor, scale, position, and the current fiction.
A GM response that sets up, reveals, or threatens a consequence.
A GM response that applies an immediate concrete consequence.
A game-specific structure that organizes related threats and their development.
A sequence showing what a threat will do if events continue or the protagonists do not intervene.
Use rules and emergent choices to discover the outcome instead of deciding it in advance.
Master of Ceremonies, Apocalypse World's facilitator title.
Monster of the Week's facilitator title.

validation_rules_for_a_pbta_rules_app: Require a specific game rules profile.
Do not assume 2d6 unless the profile declares it.
Store move trigger, roll, result branches, choices, authority, and follow-through separately.
Store modifiers with duration and qualification.
Treat relationship mechanics as game-specific typed resources.
Allow facilitatorless profiles.
Allow moves with no roll and rolls with no fictional trigger.
Allow result bands other than 6-/7-9/10+.
Record source edition and errata date for every imported rule.
Never merge move text from different games solely by matching names.

method: Prioritized official pages by Meguey and Vincent Baker, official publisher pages, and official downloadable play materials.
Used current pages to determine the status of Apocalypse World 3rd Edition development.
Used Apocalypse World 2nd Edition's official reference sheets as the stable complete classic implementation.
Used current Monster of the Week and Avatar Legends material to verify modern variations.
Paraphrased procedures rather than reproducing complete proprietary rule text.
